en: (Om) (The Dharma Text Series of the Vīraśaiva Liṅgi Brāhmaṇas |) (Volume 30)
(The Essence of Liberation) composed by Śrīmat Paramahaṃsa Maritoṇṭadārya (Śaka 1828–1907).
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
Salutations to the illustrious Sāmbasadāśiva.
{Now, the Essence of Isolation} || Verse ||
That which is one, unmanifest, infinite, worthy of praise, all-pervading, self-existent, partless, and without a second.
I bow to that stainless Liṅga, which bestows happiness in the form of the Guru. || 1 ||
Having unified this entire world, which is well-sustained by me, along with this creation;
May the sovereign guru, the bestower of Brahman, the embodiment of consciousness, the venerable Basavarya, protect us. || 2 ||

This Śaiva Tantra named Vīra, which has arisen from the root of the glorious Vedānta, which is the most excellent among the hundred pure single-locus [teachings], and which is a fierce sun for the darkness within the hearts of adversaries;

Having meditated incessantly upon the supreme Guru, the deity known as Siddhavīra, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, and having brought the phenomenal world to a state of peace, I shall act without the sense of "mine," for the sake of benefiting the world. || 3 ||
Having attained, through the grace of his Guru, the one hundred and one stages (*ekottarasthala*) in the form of the relationship with the stainless *liṅga*,
the Lord of Teachers from the Toṇṭada region speaks in prose on earth for the sake of accomplishing the realization of the bliss of the entire Self, which is the essence of liberation (*kaivalya*).
Now begins the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is the essence of liberation— the object of knowledge expounded by all the Upaniṣads for one endowed with the conduct prescribed in the *Vīratantra*. 5.
Furthermore, only the seeker of liberation who is a devotee steadfast in the Vīraśaiva vow is qualified;
and the very purpose is liberation in the form of union with the *liṅga* attained through devotion to Śiva.
The subject matter is precisely that knowledge which is expounded by all the Upaniṣads and which establishes one hundred and one topics.
The relationship between this subject matter and the treatise titled *Kaivalyasāra* is that of the object and its subject (the relation of the described and the describer). || 6 ||
Indeed, it has been stated here that only the seeker of liberation who is a devotee steadfast in the Vīraśaiva vow possesses the qualification.

If it is argued that in the absence of knowledge regarding the true nature of a Vīraśaiva, their commitment to the vows and other such characteristics would be even more difficult to discern, [the answer is that this applies only] to those who are devoted to the *Śivajñānavidyā*, which reveals the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Śiva as propounded by all the Upaniṣads.
The designation "Vīraśaiva" is mentioned in the Uttarakāmika and other [Tantras].
By the word "vi," knowledge that brings about the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul is expressed.
"Those Śaivas who take delight in that [state] are considered Vīraśaivas," because it has been so stated. || 7 ||
Now, it might be argued that liberation in the form of union (*sāyujya*) with the *liṅga* of one's own body, attained through devotion to Śiva, is indeed the sole purpose [of this work];
however, that is incorrect.

For instance, if liberation were attained through devotion to Śiva, then knowledge—which the scripture teaches as the cause of liberation by stating "liberation comes from knowledge alone"—would no longer be its cause. Furthermore, is liberation identical in nature to [the self] or distinct from it? Not the first, because it would follow that devotion lacks causality; nor the second.
If it is argued that this is not so because it would entail defects such as the destruction of non-duality and the lack of a human goal (apuruṣārthatva), we say no. || 8 ||

In the *Vātula-tantra* and other scriptures, it is stated that liberation arises from knowledge alone; however, [our view is] that devotion— which manifests as one's own independent divine play immediately following liberation in the form of the cessation of Vedic rituals caused by knowledge— is itself the direct cause of liberation.
Beyond liberation may there be the state of Śambhu.
For it has been said: "Devotion shines forth as supreme by virtue of its own independent, innate play. (9)

Otherwise, if even the knowledge that serves as a means in a traditional succession were a cause of liberation, then the mere repetition of syllables and the like would also have to be considered causes. || 10 ||
If it is asked: "What is the answer to the objection that liberation is something distinct from one's true nature?"

Listen with attention: the nature of liberation as the state of non-dual identity between the limbs (aṅga) and the Liṅga, which is characterized as being distinct from both existence and non-existence, is established by all the Āgamas, such as the Vātula. If you ask how that is so:

Śiva himself is indeed the Liṅga, and the Self (Ātman) is truly the Aṅga. The perfect union of these two—the Śiva and the Ātman—is indeed their conjunction. For the perfect union of the Liṅga and the Aṅga is always their conjunction;
this very conjunction is liberation in the form of Sāyujya, without a doubt. Thus it is said. 11.

Now, the reality of Śiva denoted by the word *sthala* is explained through statements that establish the supreme non-dual reality of Śiva, which is a compendium of the essence of all the Āgamas. (12) In this regard, first, how is the word *sthala* derived in the sense of Brahman?

Thus, warding off such a doubt, the supreme words concerning the foundational locus (adhiṣṭhāna) taught in various places throughout all the scriptures are collected and explained: "The Supreme Brahman is indeed one alone."
Characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The teachers of Śiva have respectfully declared that the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is the sacred site (sthala).
In response to the doubt as to how the word *sthala*— which in common usage denotes a different kind of place— can be applied to Brahman, he says:
Because it serves as the locus for all things, and likewise because it is their place of dissolution.
It is designated as the "ground" (sthala) of the principles (tattva), beginning with Mahat. || 14 ||
Thus, in response to the doubt as to how worldly transaction (vyavahāra) could possibly occur given that no other entity exists apart from the locus of superimposition (adhiṣṭhāna), he says:
Through the mere agitation of its own power, that ground becomes twofold.
One is declared to be the station of the Liṅga (liṅgasthala), while the other is remembered as the station of the limbs (aṅgasthala).

He dispels this doubt— namely, that according to the principle that "it is impossible for a single entity to possess two forms," it is nowhere observed that a single entity alone can be the object of cognition through differentiation— by means of an illustrative example.
Just as space is perceived through the differentiation of large jars and so forth.
And likewise, a single location is perceived through the distinction between its signs and its constituent parts.
To the question, "How can difference—imagined as something other than itself—be possible for the Supreme Self, whose nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss? he says:
Pure consciousness alone is the supreme, manifest state, characterized by truth and other such qualities.
The state of being a limb of the Liṅga is itself resorted to through the very distinction of having Śiva as one's self.

Previously it was stated that [the deity] acted merely by the agitation of his own power (*svaśakti*), whereas now it is stated that he has himself resorted to being a limb of the *liṅga*; since this appears inconsistent, he says:
Just as the ground has become divided into two parts, so too shall the power (śakti) become twofold.
Power is directly unimpeded and shares the same nature as Śiva.
Nevertheless, since there is no conceptualization of a difference between power (*śakti*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), how is difference perceived?
To this, he says:
One rests upon the region of the *liṅga*, while another rests upon the region of the body.
The power residing in the locus of the *liṅga* is proclaimed to be of the nature of the *kalās*.
The power residing in the region of the limbs is in the form of devotion and removes worldly existence.
He provides here the authority for the meaning of the word *liṅga* as stated in other tantras.
That in which and by which all that is moving and unmoving is dissolved and traversed.
This is called the *liṅga* by those who are experts in the true nature of the *liṅga*.
Having thoroughly examined the stage of the *liṅga*, he now defines the stage of the *aṅga* which follows in due order.
Toward that supreme state, which is without beginning or end and unborn, [is] the subtle mark (liṅga).
Whatever one performs with great devotion, that is certainly considered a limb [of the practice]. || 21 ||
In response to the inquiry that, as long as the true nature of the Self is not known, its very status as a limb [of the body] cannot be understood, he states the nature of the Self.
This self is solitary, pure, and eternally stainless, a portion of Śiva.
The inner self of the stainless one is eternal; therefore, the Self is itself Śiva.
To the question, "How is it possible for such a self to be a limb of Śiva?", he says:
This self is a limb of Śiva, because it has been accepted by Śiva as such.
And through the distinctions such as omniscience and so forth, it is held to consist of the limbs of Śiva. || 23 ||
He states that even by investigating the etymological derivation (*padavyutpatti*) of the word "limb" (*aṅga*), the Śiva-nature of the Self is established.
Because it goes to the immeasurable Brahman, which is pure existence alone, it is called "gam" (going).
"It is called 'rūpyate' (is transformed/manifested) as a limb," so say the wise who investigate the nature of the limbs. || 24 ||

That single locus, which was established by the passage beginning with "that which is one alone," having become twofold merely through the agitation of its own power (*svaśakti-kṣobha*), would— under the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the divisions of power (*śakti-bhakti*)—
become threefold each and each; yet, by virtue of being composed of knowledge and action, it remains one.
It is twofold and twofold.
And thus, as previously stated, the single locus of those two is conventionally designated as the "Linga-sthala," which is characterized by power (*śakti*).
But that which is distinguished by devotion is conventionally designated as "the sixfold station of the limbs" (sadaṅga-ṣaṭsthala). || 25 ||
And thus, that which is indeed one has arisen in twelve ways through mutual differentiation; now,
its intermediate subdivisions— numbering one hundred and one—
are intended as beginning with the *piṇḍa* and ending with the *jñāna-śūnya*.

In order to analyze and explain individually each of the subjects concerning the ancient traditions of all the Vīraśaiva teachers, such as Agastya, Dūrvāsas, and others, by means of a compendium of the meaning of all the Upaniṣads from the crest-jewel of those who are oceans of all branches of knowledge;
The collection of scriptural passages establishing those respective points is now being considered. || 26 ||

In this regard, although the determination of the stage of the limbs (aṅga-sthala) is indeed dependent upon the determination of the stage of the sign (liṅga-sthala), nevertheless, the stage of the sign should be determined prior to the determination of the stage of the limbs;
for it is logical that the determination of that which depends [on another] (upajīvaka) occurs only after the determination of that upon which it depends (upajīvya).

Nevertheless, since the nature of the stage of the *liṅga* (the central deity) is difficult to understand without knowledge of the nature of the stage of the *aṅgas* (the retinue), the stage of the *aṅgas* itself must be described first; thus, in accordance with this determining principle, the stage of the *sāṅga* (with its retinue) is described first. || 27 ||

Now, since there is no distinction between the two insofar as both are produced from the very same source, a determining factor— such that one has priority and the other follows immediately after— is simply not possible.

If it is argued that the primacy of Aṅga-sthala is thus accepted, [the response is: although there is no difference between the two insofar as both are produced from the same source, the very criterion for determination is that the knowledge of the nature of one depends solely upon the knowledge of the nature of the other. || 28 ||
Otherwise: egoism, power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness.
Being liberated, free from the sense of "mine," and tranquil, he is fit for becoming Brahman. || 29 ||
With a self that has become Brahman and is serene, he neither grieves nor desires.
Being equal toward all beings, one attains supreme devotion to Me.
Thus, there would also be a violation of the sequence of priority and posteriority. || 30 ||
Therefore, since it has been established that the stage of the limbs (aṅga-sthala) must be described first,
the stage of the body (piṇḍa-sthala)— which constitutes a specific subdivision of that [stage] and serves as its basis— is now described. || 31 ||

In this context, one whose sins have been exhausted by virtue of meritorious deeds performed over many lifetimes, and who possesses a pure internal organ in his final body— that very self designated as the "piṇḍa" (the physical form), being the Supreme Brahman residing within it, is called the "piṇḍasthala" (the station of the body). || 32 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
Oil is in sesame seeds, clarified butter in curd, water in rivers, and fire in flint-stones.
Thus is that Self grasped within the self by one who perceives it through truth and austerity. || 33 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
A sprout [arises] from a beautiful seed, and fire [arises] from a sun-gem.
Just as it is accomplished in water and in the moonstone, so too is it accomplished within one's own body.

When such a desire arises to demonstrate the reality consisting of both the manifest (sakala) and the unmanifest (niṣkala) abiding within one's own interior in that very Supreme Brahman, the knowledge that subsequently arises regarding the self as a physical body (piṇḍa) is called the stage of "knowledge of the body" (piṇḍajñāna). || 35 ||
Having taken up the eye of knowledge from the Amṛtanāda Upaniṣad, one should extract the Supreme like fire.
"I am that Brahman, which is immovable, partless, and peaceful"—thus it is remembered.
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad.
Bodiless, yet abiding within bodies that are themselves unstable.
"Having realized the Self as great and all-pervading, the wise man does not grieve. Thus it has been said in the Vāsiṣṭha.
O Rāma, let there be no further deliberation for you as to "whence comes this illusion?"
And let this be your deliberation: "How may I abandon her? (38)

The great-souled one, possessing such knowledge of the *piṇḍa*, having thoroughly investigated the reality of both the manifest (*sakala*) and the unmanifest (*niṣkala*), and when the realization of the rejectability of the transmigratory world in its manifest form has arisen, that which follows is called the stage of the rejectability of the transmigratory world. (Maitreyopaniṣad 39)

O Blessed One, what is the use of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures in this body which is defiled by bone, skin, sinew, marrow, flesh, semen, blood, and phlegm; a conglomeration of feces, urine, wind, bile, and phlegm; foul-smelling and devoid of essence? Thus it has been said in the Purāṇa:
In this conglomeration of flesh, blood, pus, feces, urine, sinews, marrow, and bones;
If that fool feels attachment to the body, he will find it even in hell.

Immediately after such loathing for saṃsāra, since the direct realization of one's own true nature is impossible in the absence of the teacher’s instruction, and once one has approached a teacher for that purpose,
the stage of the teacher’s compassion is described. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12–13)

"For the sake of realizing that, one should approach a teacher alone, with sacrificial fuel in hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman. Furthermore, in the *Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad*:
"Now, what indeed could dry up these other great oceans, or cause the falling of mountain peaks?"
In this cycle of existence characterized by such things as the shaking or falling of the Pole Star,
the sinking of trees, or the displacement of the earth from its place— what [is there for the gods]?
"I am that"— in such a world as this, what [is there]?

"Since we see that one who relies solely on the enjoyment of sensual pleasures repeatedly revolves within desire, you ought to lift us up; O Blessed One, you are our refuge in this saṃsāra, which is like a frog situated in a blind well. Thus it was said in the Vākyavṛtti.
By which one may be liberated from the bondage of existence without effort.
Therefore, O Blessed One, please tell me that in brief and in its entirety out of compassion. (45)

Thus, for that very Great Soul endowed with profound compassion, having abandoned the attributes of the gross body composed of the five elements and having performed the wearing of the *liṅga* upon the body which has become a means for practicing righteous conduct (*sadācāra*), immediately thereafter—
This is called the place for wearing the *liṅga*, as stated in the seventh chapter of the Ṛgveda.
Your purifier is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati; as the sovereign lord, you encompass our limbs from every side.
One whose body is not heated does not enjoy that which is raw; only those who have taken refuge in it and are bearers of it have attained it. 47.
It has been stated likewise in the Kāmikāgama:
"Rik," he says; "Your filter is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati."
Therefore, that pure Śaiva liṅga, which is free from all affliction, should be worn.
Like a king whose body has not been tempered, his essence remains devoid of refinement.
One who is devoid of initiation shall not directly attain the supreme liṅga.
Furthermore, in the Brahmopaniṣad:
One should hold that which is the imperishable, supreme Brahman to be the Sūtra.
They say it is called a "sūtra" because it indicates; indeed, the name "sūtra" refers to the supreme state.
By upholding that Sūtra, one shall become neither impure from remnants of food nor unclean.
Regarding this matter, it is stated in the Yogajagama:
But because it is thoroughly woven throughout, it is continuous even amidst all things.
Because it indicates the Supreme Lord, the Sūtra is called the Liṅga.
Furthermore, in the Bṛhatkālottara:
Vows that are difficult to perform here, and those ascetic penances which are fierce;
All those [sins] become diminished by the wearing of the Śivaliṅga. || 52 ||
Likewise, in the Śivarahasya:
With a completely pure mind, he was firm in his vows through self-restraint.
Bearing the Liṅga upon the heads of Śiva, one attains Śiva himself. || 53 ||
Likewise, it is also stated in the Vātula:
He who possesses no worldly disposition, as well as shame and the like;
That devotee, steadfast and blessed, should wear the Liṅga everywhere.
In that very same [text].
But one who is steadfast in the sole vow of servitude has transcended the worldly state.
One who is self-controlled should wear the Śivaliṅga and worship it with a disciplined mind.

Thus, for one who is perfected in the wearing of the *liṅga*, the wearing of the sacred ash—which is the very nature of the light of consciousness inseparable from the Supreme Brahman—must be performed; this very rule is called the "place" (*sthala*) for the wearing of the *vibhūti*. || 56 ||
In the Jābālopaniṣad it is said: "By the wearing of the sacred ash (vibhūti), one attains oneness with Brahman;

he is the light of ash, he is the light of ash. By the wearing of the sacred ash, one enjoys absolute liberation (kaivalya); he is the light of ash, he is the light of ash. By the wearing of the sacred ash alone, one also attains immortality."
This indeed is the light of ashes; this indeed is the light of ashes. || 57 ||

Thus, when the wearing of rudrākṣas— which has been undertaken through the performance of the ritual of consecration with the ashes of great knowledge and is perfected by the rite of the liṅga, and which arises from the eye of Śiva-knowledge— has been performed, that immediately thereafter is called the "place for wearing rudrākṣas. (Jābāla Upaniṣad).
"He who wears this rudrākṣa becomes one who has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrtha);

he becomes a bearer of all the Vedas; he becomes a performer of all sacrifices; he becomes identical with the essence of all the Vedas; he is truly the supreme Śiva—he is the supreme Śiva. (59) [In that very same work:]
Even while committing sin, a human being who wears a rudrākṣa crosses over all evil;
thus it is stated in the Mānava Purāṇa.
Even if a person commits a sin while wearing a rudrākṣa, he is purified.
For the Jābāla Śruti declares: "He crosses over all evil. (61)
Thus, for one who possesses the marks [of a devotee], who wears the *vibhūti* and *rudrākṣa*,

who is devoted to the constant worship of the *liṅga*, and who is endowed with the *liṅga*, the recitation (*japa*) of the five-syllabled mantra accompanied by the *praṇava* is necessary; immediately following this—
This is called the site of the five syllables. In the Yajurveda, within the Śatarudrīya, it says: "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya ca. (62–63)
Likewise, it is stated in the *Śivajñānavidyā*: "The limb (*aṅga*) is the word 'namas'; this is Śiva;
the linga is the word 'saṃbandha' (connection); this is declared to be the word for *māyā*."
This mantra, the king of mantras of the Vedas and Agamas, speaks for the purpose of awakening the three steps of the union between the Linga and the body.

Thus, having worn the vibhūti and rudrākṣas and having recited the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣarī), for one who is devoted to the daily worship of the liṅga, the performance of the ritual acts with all their constituent parts is described next as the "Stage of Devotion" (bhaktisthala) in response to the inquiry as to how it should be done. (Vṛddhajābāla Upaniṣad, 65).
Therefore, having applied sacred ash and Rudrākṣa beads, and having worshipped Rudra with the Rudrānuvākas. || 66 ||

Having praised the Supreme Lord with such passages as "Rudra is indeed one alone; he does not stand for a second," and contemplating him constantly through reasoned arguments, one should meditate upon him. Thereafter, through the severing of all bonds of bondage, one becomes liberated, becomes eternally blissful, no longer remains a transmigrating being, and becomes the very nature of Śiva.
He becomes the very nature of Śiva; he becomes the very nature of Śiva. And so it is stated in the *Śivādvaita*:
"Through devotion to service, one becomes Śiva himself, a Śiva-yogin."
He who performs worship with a joyful mind is called a devotee. Likewise, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
Devotion belongs only to the liberated one; it never belongs to the bound one.
For liberation belongs only to the devotee, never to the non-devotee; thus it is said in the Vātula.
There is a partial convergence of serenity, devotion, and liberation.
"Even liberation might be produced; the remaining two are considered its producers. (70) In that very same [text]:
Clarity of mind is declared to be the father, and devotion is said to be the mother.
From the state of oneness between these two, the maiden Muktikanyā was born. (Skanda Purāṇa)
Having established the vital breath (prāṇa) within the liṅga, one should likewise establish the Śāmbhava-liṅga within the vital breath.
If one makes the mind incorporate the body and does not think of anything at all; || 72 ||
This is called "internal devotion" by the yogis of Śiva.
The life of one in whom that [impurity] resides is like a rotten seed. || 73 ||
In that very place: "What is the use of saying much more here? This is the supreme [teaching], more secret than the secret."
There is no doubt that devotion to Śiva exists; one endowed with it is liberated. || 74 ||
Furthermore, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
Devotion to the deity arises from grace, and grace is born of devotion.
Just as the seed is from the sprout, or the sprout is from the seed.
And devotion preceded by serene faith is the means that brings about liberation.
That cannot be attained by men in a single lifetime.
In that regard: "For those who have been purified through many births and who follow the Śruti and Smṛti..."
Maheśvara is pleased with those who are dispassionate and awakened.
When it becomes serene, one is liberated; being liberated, one becomes equal to Śiva.
Even for that mortal who possesses little merit, after three births— || 78 ||
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Various pilgrimages to sacred fords and diverse sacrifices have been performed.
Therefore, devotion toward Śiva arises for them only after thousands of births.
Furthermore, in the Brahmagītā:
I am not pleased by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice.
I am pleased by even a slight fragment of devotion; one quickly attains the supreme state.
In that very same [text].
Neither by ritual action, nor by austerity, nor by recitations, nor by meditative absorptions.
I am not to be won over by knowledge nor by charity, without faith.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Or even the accumulation of both auspicious and inauspicious karmas.
Devotion reduces everything to ashes, just as fire consumes fuel.
In the Śaivaratnākara.
Association with virtuous devotees and the complete absence of evil company.
Through these two, men's supreme devotion to Śiva increases. (83)

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to what the nature of the relationship between the body and vital breaths— acting as servants— and the devotee who has attained the state of true devotion is like, the "state of both" (ubhayasthala) is described immediately thereafter. || 84 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as he does for the Divine..."
For these meanings explained here shine forth clearly to that high-souled one. || 85 ||
The same has been stated in the *Tattvasāra*:
Having known the true Guru to be Śiva eternally, the wise man should perform his worship.
For he who, having Śiva as his sole refuge, performs [the rite] in both forms [of the deity]. (86)

Thus, for the devotee who possesses knowledge of the relationship between both the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* in both contexts, when there arises the inquiry as to how the contemplation (*vicāra*) upon the Guru, the *liṅga*, the *jaṅgama*, and the *bhūta* occurs within the states of body and mind, the "Stage of Various Attainments" (*vividhasampattisthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 87 ||

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, it is stated that through the recognition of Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains universal sovereignty in the third state, being one whose desires are entirely fulfilled. It has been stated likewise in the Vātula Tantra.
The same equanimity that one has toward the Guru and the Deity should likewise be maintained toward the Śiva-yoginī.
That alone is the threefold perfection for those who possess the sovereignty of consciousness. 89.

Thus, for the devotee who has attained the state endowed with the threefold perfection, when there arises the inquiry as to how the distinctions between the guru, the *liṅga*, the *jaṅgama*, the *prasāda*, and devotion manifest within the transformations of body, mind, and knowledge, the "fourfold stage of the essence" (*caturvidhasārāya-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 90 ||
In the *Pārāśara-śruti*, it is said: "They run forward; the world of heaven is in front.
He consecrates them with four [verses]; there are four meters (*chandas*); by means of the meters, he causes them to go to the world of heaven. Thus it has been stated in the *Śivarahasya*.
This [grace] is of one and the same form toward the Śivācāryas, guests, and even in the temple of the Lord.
That devotion, which is declared to have fourfold essence, is unswerving.

Thus, the Great-Souled One, endowed with the fourfold excellence of essence, place, and time, having established the worship of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama, for the sake of instructing all devotees in what is beneficial, [proceeded as follows].
Immediately after [the section on] Truth, the place where adjuncts (upādhi) are introduced is mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
There are three pillars of dharma: sacrifice, study, and giving—thus it is stated in the Kāṭhaka Śruti.
But he who eats here without having first offered food as an oblation to his guests, indeed eats only sin. || 95 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Śivarahasya:
And, O lady of excellent hips, asceticism, sacrifices, ritual acts, and the like, all come to an end.
O lady of excellent hips, the oblation offered into the mouths of heroes is never exhausted. || 96 ||
Furthermore, in the Śaiva Purāṇa, there is a verse:
I do not eat that sacrificial offering spread out by the sacrificer, nor this [oblation] soaked in ghee offered through the mouth of the fire-eater;
for my satisfaction comes from what moves about month after month from the mouths of living beings. Indeed, my nourishment comes from the ripening of one's own past actions performed with diligence:
the grinding, the breaking, the hearth, the water-jar, and the sweeping.
A householder has five slaughterhouses; by what means is liberation not attained? || 98 ||
The duty toward the gods, the duty toward the guru, and the duty toward the Gaṇas are for the yogin.
One who digs up a mound or breaks it into pieces is not tainted by sins. || 99 ||
Likewise, it is stated in the Śātātapa-smṛti:
One should not cook food for one's own sake, but rather cook it for the sake of the deities.
He who cooks for his own sake alone is called a slayer of a Brahmin.
Furthermore, in the Śivarahasya:
For the sake of the Liṅga and for the sake of the Jaṅgama, [prepare] the excellent, special cooked offering.
Food cooked for one's own sake becomes equal to dog meat. || 101 ||
In the Brahmagītā:
Giving is considered to be of two kinds: that which is bestowed and that which is withdrawn.
The teachers have declared that the active [path] (pravṛtta) is the means for accomplishing lordship over the gods and other such states. || 102 ||
In the Śivadharmottara:
Therefore, having recognized one who is a most worthy recipient—a devotee of Śiva free from all taint—[one should bestow it upon him].
To him everything should be given by one who desires inexhaustible fruit.
In the Śaivaratnākara.
And whatever is given to another, bypassing a devotee of Śiva;
That gift would be fruitless, and he shall fall into hell. || 104 ||
In the Śivarahasya:
By means of every distinction of conduct and by every distinction of vows.
By virtue of the excellence of all my moral conduct, I am Śivadāsa, the most excellent.

Having thus instructed all devotees on the commencement of devotion, the Great-Souled One himself, disregarding all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and being free from such adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), became intent upon service;
in response to the inquiry as to how this was so, the following section is called "The Place of Unconditional Giving" (*Nirupādhidānasthala*). || 106 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.

He who is the sovereign of the gods, upon whom the worlds are supported, who is the lord of this biped and quadruped world—to which god shall we offer worship with oblation? Thus it is said in the Śivarahasya.
Considering all my work as belonging to my Lord and Master, and impelled by the Lord, [I perform it].
That action which is performed for the sake of a worthy recipient is an action free from limiting conditions.
Furthermore, in the Bhagavadgītā:
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who cannot repay it;
That gift is unconditional when given at the right place, at the right time, and to a worthy recipient. || 109 ||
In the Vātula Tantra.
If one says, "This is mine; it is for you," yet does not give away any object whatsoever.
"This gift, consisting of the thought 'this is yours' or 'to you,' is declared to be pure. (110)
In that very same [text].
One should constantly fulfill the commitments with one's wealth, life, and sense of self-importance.
O Goddess, it is said here that the purification of the path occurs through meditation at the three junctions of the day.
Thus, having become free from all conditions (*nirupādhika*), the Great Soul (*mahātman*) becomes intent on service through the relationship of master and servant;
when non-duality has been attained regarding his own performed devotion and the accepted object, that which follows is called the stage of spontaneous giving (*sahajadāna*). || 112 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all this has been declared as the threefold Brahman;
likewise it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
The giver, the gift, the object to be given, and the recipient are indeed Śiva himself.
"I am not the cause"—this is declared to be the stainless gift. || 114 ||
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world.
Śiva performs all that; he is Śiva, and he is indeed I myself. || 115 ||
Kapila said:
He who [spends] wealth acquired through righteous means solely out of devotion to Śiva...
One who gives while free from attachment—that gift is known as innate (sahaja). || 116 ||
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Śikṣā]:
He in whom everything is complete within the reality that is the Supreme Bliss, whose nature is consciousness free from all limiting conditions—he is Śaṅkara himself. || 117 ||

[Thus ends the first chapter, named the Stage of Devotion (*bhaktasthalam*), in the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is an exposition of the *Śrutimālā* consisting of one hundred and one stages, titled *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*, composed by the illustrious *Paramaśivayogirāṭ* and wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*) Śrī Toṇṭadārya.]
[Now begins the second chapter.]

Salutations to Śrī Śiva. Thus, having resorted to the station of the devotee (bhaktasthala), having forgotten the relationship of master and servant, and having— following the description of the majesty established in one’s own true nature— recalled the conduct by way of steadfast devotion, one attains the state of oneness (sāmarasya) wherein all distinctions have vanished.

In response to the inquiry "How so?", the section on Māheśvara is stated immediately thereafter. (1) O Śrī Rudra, those who are the lords of beings, who are hairless and wear matted locks. (2) Likewise, in the *Uttarakāmika*:
The entire host of deities, beginning with Brahmā, is perpetually deluded by Māyā.
But it is incapable of bestowing liberation, as it is associated with the defects of decay and excess.
The Blessed One, the sole Great Lord, is liberated from time immemorial.
And that god who is the giver of liberation is indeed remembered as Māheśvara. || 4 ||
By Brahmā and others who are mostly defiled, [this is offered] to the stainless Supreme Lord.
He who cannot endure the expression of equality is indeed called a Māheśvara.
The perfections of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others are characterized by decay and excellence.
A hero devoted to Maheśvara always regards [all things] with his intellect as if they were mere blades of grass.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
At all times, devotion to Śiva and the worship of the Liṅga and the Jaṅgama are [the path].
The vow of a single wife, the great vow of the heroic devotee of Maheśvara.
In the Śaivaratnākara.
That alone is declared to be the *liṅga*, for he indeed possesses the conduct of the *liṅga*.
By that very mark of conduct, the person who possesses the mark is a devotee of Maheśvara.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the non-difference from the Liṅga residing in the limbs occurs for a Māheśvara who has made a firm resolve regarding the rules, vows, and so forth at the site of Māheśvara, the "Stage of Devotion to the Liṅga" (liṅganiṣṭhāsthala) is described immediately thereafter. || 9 ||
In the Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad.
"Śiva alone, the bringer of auspiciousness, is to be meditated upon, having abandoned everything else"—thus concludes the Atharvaṇa Śruti;
it has been stated likewise in the Śaiva Purāṇa.
The liberator from saṃsāra is Śiva himself in person, and no other.
And all other deities are merely bestowers of worldly enjoyments.
Abandoning everything else, Śiva alone is the bringer of auspiciousness.
"The Supreme Atharva Veda indeed declares that He is the object of meditation. (12)
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
That which is [attained] through prostration, sight, touch, worship, and so forth, performed with regularity;
The worship of the Śiva-liṅga is proclaimed as "liṅga-niṣṭhā" (devotion fixed on the liṅga). || 13 ||
Furthermore, in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
That alone is the supreme abode; that alone is the highest goal in this world.
That alone is the supreme limit here, the culmination of the signs of Śiva.
Likewise, it was stated by Brahmā in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
His form is threefold: gross, subtle, and beyond that.
It is visible to the immortals such as ourselves in its gross form, and to yogis in its subtle form.
But beyond that is that which is eternal, consciousness, bliss, and imperishable.
That vow is to be seen by the faithful who are devoted to it, intent upon it, and dedicated to it.
Furthermore, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
Devotion to the Liṅga, worship of the Liṅga, and indeed the wearing of the Liṅga.
Accepting the grace of the Liṅga and listening to the teachings concerning the Liṅga with reverence.
Meditation is the Linga, the mind is the Linga; the entire universe consists of the Linga.

Thus, a devotee of Maheśvara who is established in the *liṅga*, being intensely attached to that *liṅga*, regards his own previous births, the state of being a living soul, the worldly manifoldness, and his former stages of life as false; once they have been discarded, that which follows is called the "place of discarding the former refuge. || 18 ||
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself; in his lineage no one ignorant of Brahman remains;
he crosses over sorrow, he crosses over evil, and being liberated from the knots of the heart, he becomes immortal. || 19 ||
Furthermore, in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad:
Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality. || 20 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Skanda Purāṇa:
They say that ignorance comes first; existence is beginningless and has that as its substratum.
All that must be discarded with effort by the wise man. || 21 ||
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
But he who has been initiated should perform his own preliminary rites before the *śrāddha* and other ceremonies.
All of that becomes fruitless for him, and he violates the sacred pledge (samaya). || 22 ||
In the Śivarahasya:
The twilight prayers, meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, and libations to the ancestors.
However, one who bears the Śiva-linga should not perform any of those practices of the elders.

Thus, having discarded the notion of Maheśvara from the previous substratum and having understood that the *liṅga* is [the Self], when the bliss of that *liṅga* is expressed through separate speech, one attains a state of duality; or, upon the cessation of that speech, the stage immediately following is called the "place for the elimination of verbal duality. || 24 ||
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad: "Existing in the midst of ignorance, yet considering themselves wise and learned, these fools wander about like the blind led by the blind;
existing in many ways within ignorance, they think, 'We have achieved our purpose.'"
Thus do the ignorant imagine; [as stated] in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. Thus it is likewise stated in the Sūtasamhitā:
Two birds, known as the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa), are situated within this body.
Of those two, the individual soul (jīva) experiences the fruit of karma, not the Great Lord (maheśvara). || 27 ||
Likewise, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
If one were to say to an ignorant person who has only slightly awakened that "everything is Brahman," [he would fail to understand].
He was cast by him into the nets of the great hells. || 28 ||
Furthermore, in the Viśvasāda: In the [text] called Viśvasāda:
Hara, the Lord of All, is the self of all existing things.
If that [Self] exists yet remains unknown, alas, how could non-duality come to be? || 29 ||
Likewise, it is so with Padmanābha.
Rudra is indeed one alone; there is no second whatsoever.
This is the realization of non-duality; any other that is cited is useless.
Having thus refuted the duality of speech and realized that the Liṅga alone is complete in every limb,
Maheśvara finds no occasion to either invoke or dismiss it;
since both invocation and dismissal have been set aside, this stage is thereafter called the "Refutation of Invocation."
31 || In the Praśnopaniṣad ||
That body of yours which is established in speech, that which is in the ear, and that which is in the eye.
And whatever auspicious continuity exists in the mind, maintain that; do not deviate from it.
It has been stated likewise in the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi:
When the great preceptor bestows the Liṅga conjoined with the Śiva-kalā.
Since that time, Śiva has remained there; what need is there for an invocation here?
In that very place.
Śiva is eternally present within well-refined lingas.
In that case, no invocation should be performed, as it would contradict the proper practice. || 34 ||
Again, in that very same place:
One should not perform the invocation nor the dismissal in one's own personal *liṅga*.
"One who is constantly devoted to the Liṅga—this is the firm conclusion of the scripture. (35)
Furthermore, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
O Goddess, it is latent impression that is summoned, and it is latent impression alone that is released.
In the ultimate sense, there is neither invocation nor dismissal for the Deity.
Furthermore, in the *Tantrasāra*:
O Goddess, from where is it led away, or from where is it not released?
For he abides among yogis through the distinctions of gross, subtle, and so forth. || 37 ||

Thus, for the devotee of Maheśvara who has abandoned both invocation and dismissal, when the entire phenomenal world manifested through the eight bodies is known to be false, the stage immediately following that realization is called the "place of the dissolution of the eight forms. || 38 ||
In the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa Upaniṣad.
He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, and who controls the earth from within—
He is the Inner Controller, the Immortal Self. He who dwells in the waters, yet is within the waters, whom the waters do not know, whose body is the waters...
He who dwells within the body, yet is other than the body, whom the body does not know, whose body this is, and who controls the body from within—he is the Inner Controller, the Immortal Self.
He who, dwelling in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—
he is the Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who, dwelling in wind, is within wind,
whom wind does not know, whose body is wind, who...

He who, dwelling within the wind, controls the wind from within, yet whom the wind does not know, whose body is the wind, and who controls the wind from within—he is the Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who, dwelling within space...
[dwelling within the moon... he is the Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

This one who dwells within the moon, whom the moon does not know, whose body is the moon, and who controls the moon from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who dwells in the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun... [and so forth].

He who dwells within the sun, yet is other than the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun, and who controls the sun from within—he is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the Immortal. He who dwells within the self (ātman), yet is other than the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, and who controls the self from within—he is the Inner Controller, the Immortal. 39. And so forth.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
Likewise, the potter and other such agents do not themselves become the jar or other such effects.
For Īśāna, who cuts away the earth and so forth, is indeed entirely other than the earth and the rest.
In that very same [text].
Just as the embodied self is said to be distinct from the body and so forth;
Likewise, there is a formal Lord (mūrtimān īśvara) who is distinct from the eight forms (mūrty-aṣṭaka). || 41 ||
And so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The Blessed Lord Śiva is not endowed with qualities such as fragrance, unlike the earth and other elements.
And just as water does not possess the nature of a flowing stream, so too is the all-pervading Lord.
Just as fire is hot, yet it does not move horizontally like the wind.
Śiva, the supreme consciousness, is not like space in the case of sound. || 43 ||
Like the moon and sun, he remains unwearied; like a pillar, he never wavers.
The Supreme Lord has no connection with the qualities of Māyā and so forth, as the Self does not have.

Thus, when the eightfold form has been relinquished by Maheśvara, and having known Śiva as "full of refuge" (śaraṇapūrṇa) and established Him, one says "Śiva is full of the world" (jagatpūrṇa); once the negation of the term "all-pervading" (sarvagata) has been performed, that stage is subsequently called the "negation of the all-pervading" (sarvagatanirasana).
45 || In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad ||
He is not followed by anything, for this person is indeed unattached. || 46 ||
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
For the supreme Śruti declares: "Indeed, this is unattached."
Therefore, the self, being merely designated by means of actions, is not bound by them.
For the Śruti indeed declares the direct Brahmanhood of the Self, whose nature is consciousness.
Furthermore, in the Śivagītā:
How can there be omnipresence for Śiva, the Supreme Self?
"For this person is indeed unattached," so says the exalted Śruti. (48)
Likewise, in the Śivadharmottara:
How can Śiva, the Supreme Person, be omnipresent?
Everything is insentient and perishable, while Śiva is the mass of consciousness and bliss. || 49 ||
Furthermore, for this very reason, it is stated in the Śrī Rudropaniṣad:
O Rudra, that form of yours which is auspicious, non-terrible, and which does not appear as evil—
With that most auspicious body of yours, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor.
It has been stated likewise in the Śaiva Purāṇa.
The Liṅga is said to be the body of Śiva, while the Mūrti is remembered as his Ghoratanu (terrible) form.
And among those devotees who are free from evil, the auspicious form [of Śiva] resides between the two.
Those who wear the *liṅga* shine as the remaining disciples of the Supreme Lord. || 51 ||
Furthermore, in the Vātula:
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is non-terrible and does not cause sin—[with that, protect us].
Because he is praised with the Yajus, therefore the devotee of Śiva is freed from sin.
Furthermore, from the *Śivayogapradīpikā*:
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which shines eternally among your own [attendants].
"The eternal Śruti declares that Aghorā is the destroyer of sin. (53)
When the cause has arrived, the conduct [is as follows].
O Blessed One, we have heard that your body is free from evil; you are renowned among the disciplined as one who is sinless.
Therefore, I conclude that you have abandoned your own devotees and are instructing others instead. || 54 ||

Thus, when it is made known that one who has cast off all notions of a pervasive Maheśvara realizes that within this phenomenal world (prapañca) there is nothing apart from Śiva, and that without Śiva the very appearance of the world would not exist— thereby reaching the certainty that even while remaining in that world, he remains as if not remaining at all— immediately thereafter the stage called "Consisting of Śiva and the World" is described.
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
Brahman alone is this immortal reality, spread out in front, behind, to the south, to the north, below, and above;
Brahman alone is this entire universe, the most excellent. Furthermore:
In the Uttarātāpanīya Upaniṣad.
For this Lord is all-pervading, consisting of action and knowledge; indeed, everything is composed of Śiva, and all living beings are composed of Śiva. Thus it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, which are inherent to Him.

He has no master in the world, nor any ruler, nor even any gender-mark (liṅga). And so it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Whatever exists in this entire world, moving and unmoving, is presided over by Śiva."
His power is pure, innate, and surpasses all others. || 59 ||
Furthermore, in the Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad:
For the single Self of all beings is indeed situated within every being.
He is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water. || 60 ||
It has been stated exactly thus in the Yogaśāstra.
For the single Self of all beings alone is established within every body.
He is seen as one and indeed as many, like the moon reflected in water. || 61 ||
Furthermore, in the Saura Purāṇa:
Consciousness, entirely free from all limiting adjuncts, is the all-pervading Śiva.
For this entire universe is indeed that very [Brahman]; therefore, nothing other than it exists.
Thus, having understood that Śiva alone is capable of both the form of the universe and the form distinct from the universe,

and having embraced that Śiva within himself while remaining in the state of Āheśvara, [the Lord asks] how such a Śiva remains as the embodied body of a devotee while maintaining his distinction; and in response to this inquiry, immediately thereafter—
This is called the Bhaktadehika-liṅga-sthala. [From] the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, in verse.
Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; without eyes, he sees; without ears, he hears.
"He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the Great Puruṣa.
Thus it is said in the Śivarahasya.
He who is the refuge for Śiva’s body shall himself become Śiva, the very embodiment of refuge.
One who takes refuge in Śiva’s face will truly become Śiva himself, whose very face is the refuge.
Furthermore, in the Śivasūtra:
Just as Śiva, although omnipresent, presides specifically over the *liṅga*.
In the same way, the manifestation of Śiva-nature is held to occur precisely within those who are devoted. || 66 ||

[Thus ends the second chapter, named the Māheśvara-sthala, in the Kaivalyasāra, which is a commentary on the Śrutimālā of one hundred and one topics, titled Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī, composed by the venerable Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of yogins of the illustrious Paramaśiva and wandering ascetic teacher.]
[The Third Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva.
Thus, having performed the prescribed conduct at the site of Māheśvara, the Great Soul, possessing the state of identity between the devotee and the Liṅga,
thereafter [discusses] the distinction in practice with an attentive face.
To the question "In what manner?", it is stated immediately thereafter: "the place of grace. (1)
In the Jābāla Upaniṣad.
They eat what has been eaten by Rudra; they drink what has been drunk by Rudra; they smell what has been smelled by Rudra.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
The disciplined and the tranquil indeed eat only what has been eaten by Rudra.
For they smell only what has been smelled, and they drink only what has been drunk.
Furthermore, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
When food is pure, the mind becomes pure; when the mind is pure, mindfulness becomes steadfast.
Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is liberation from all knots. || 4 ||
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Whatever food a person eats, that same food belongs to his deity.
It has been stated exactly so in the Vātula.
This is the determination of the principles concerning the three: the world, the individual soul, and the Lord.
The three [types of] offerings of leftover food are determined in sequence. || 6 ||
The world, consisting of the body and so forth, is a remnant characterized by delusion.
The one who identifies with that food is the individual soul (jīva), characterized by transmigratory existence.
Lord Prasāda is the manifest embodiment of the characteristics of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
The meter is Vṛtta.
Grace is devoid of beginning and end; it is itself of an indivisible nature, characterized as that which remains.

Free from conceptual construction and abiding in perfect purity, this is his innate power arising from his own nature; therein substances such as food dissolve, and that which is reached is understood from whence it comes.
That linga is [known] as Prasāda, and for that very reason, it is indeed grace (prasāda).
Either by means of worship through the gateway [of the officiant], or by means of the offering of the *liṅga* oneself.
This single term "prasāda" is used figuratively to denote both [the Lord] and devotion. || 10 ||
Food is that which has the form of an object; its production is declared to be conceptual construction (kalpanā).
For the offering is indeed the dissolution of the mantra; know that taking up is its grasping. || 11 ||
The meter is Vṛtta.
The food and other offerings contained within a vessel, once presented, constitute that portion which has entered the receptacle.
If it is offered to the Liṅga and placed in a vessel, it should indeed be presented as being contained within that receptacle.
That which is the primordial butter, consisting of clarified butter, when heated in the mouth of fire, becomes its own [essence].
In whatever manner it may be, the first food that has been offered at the mouth of the Liṅga and consists of the nature of divine grace (prasāda); || 13 ||
Just as when the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated, that which remains by itself is indeed what persists.
In the same way, when the state of being an object has vanished from grace, the reality itself remains by its own nature.
There is no state of being leavings, nor any state of being forbidden, in the supreme and most pure direct grace.
Listen to the truth regarding the grace of wealth: once that wealth has been enjoyed, there is indeed no possibility of its return. || 15 ||
If grace were to consist in the state of being leftover or forbidden, then grace would not truly exist at all.
Because of its non-existence, it has no characteristic mark; there is no teacher, nor is there a gradual descent [of grace]. || 16 ||
Medicine should be taken for the sake of the disease, and likewise for the sake of one's own [mental] defects.
"This grace of Śiva is to be served"—this is the supreme state of the Śaivas. (Verse 17) [In Vṛtta meter]
By those who are unconditioned, selfless, beyond the senses and the elements, bodiless, indifferent to their own interests, and free from desire.
That which is seen, heard, touched, or enjoyed, as well as that which is smelled and so forth, and what is known as "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa)—
all this is [perceived] by us who possess the six sense-bases, yet who are beyond the senses, free from objects, and devoid of desire.
Whatever has been eaten is indeed not considered leavings (ucchiṣṭa), nor is it forbidden, nor is it defiled. (Verse 19)

His body is the *liṅga* called conduct (*ācāra*), his self is the *liṅga* of dignity (*gaurava*), his vital breath is the *Śiva-liṅga*, and likewise, the collection of his senses is itself [the *liṅga*].

It has been declared that there are the mobile liṅgas, as well as the stationary liṅgas, the temple-liṅgas, and the liṅgas of the six sacred sites; what more can I tell you, O Great Liṅga, who are the embodiment of all these? || 20 ||
That which has emerged from the pestle, the mortar, the hearth, the water-jar, the sesame press, and the mouth [of the teacher].
Nothing at all is defiled in the world; rather, that which originates from the mouth of the Guru, the Liṅga, the Jaṅgama, and so forth, is what is defiled.
On this point, in another Tantra:
The followers of Manu maintain that there is no fault in eating together with women.
The wicked-souled do not accept the food offered by my devotees as a mark of grace. (Āryā verse)
At the beginning and at the end, there are two types of impurity: that of the boiled rice and that of the leavings.
Having abandoned the grace of Śiva, he enjoys that for which another becomes the gracious one. || 23 ||
Birth-impurity is declared to be a sin (pātaka), and a sin is a great transgression (kilbiṣa).
Therefore, having abandoned that first impurity (sūtaka), one should engage in enjoyment.
And through the grace of the Guru Śiva, who is the embodiment of the ultimate reality and the source of right conduct.
O Great One, that which has been smelled, drunk, seen, touched, heard, and remembered—worship Your own mind.
(Verse 25) [In Vṛtta meter]
The vessel is the body, the receptacle is the sense organs, and this individual soul is the substance; that which is the food is [the object of experience].
Having offered it with devotion to the Supreme Liṅga, partake of that prasāda as its subordinate remnant.
26 || In the Yogajagama:
He is the knower of bliss, he is the lord of yogis, and he alone is the knower of the reality of the scriptures.
He who acts with his own senses while his mind is dedicated to Śiva, [attains success]. (27)
In the Śivarahasya.
One who possesses the Liṅga and is united with the Liṅga enjoys all objects offered to the Liṅga.
One who renounces without attachment is called "gracious" (prasādī). || 28 ||
In that very same [text].
There are many worshippers, hundreds of thousands in number, who are devoted.
Only two or three are worthy of my grace, certainly not five or six.

Thus, when there is a desire to know how the greatness of the Guru— who is embraced by the limbs of one who accepts the grace of the gracious [Lord] through the grace of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama— is manifested, the subsequent section is called the "Section on the Greatness of the Guru" (Gurumāhātmyasthalam). This is stated in the Atharvaṇa Veda.

Having assumed a body shaped like a kadamba bud for the supreme welfare of the universe, he bears this form for the benefit of the world through the Vedas and other scriptures, and through mantras beginning with the Praṇava, for the performance of rites such as ritual action. This very Self, who is consciousness, is Rudra;
he is moving, two-armed, two-eyed, two-footed, and one-headed—the one Rudra in the form of the Teacher. || 31 ||
And so it is stated in the Vīrāgama:
The eye on the forehead, the digit of the moon, and also the two arms.
O Maheśvarī, I exist within, having assumed the form of the Guru.
In the Laiṅgya [Tantra].
I consider the lotus-feet of the Guru to be even more precious than touch itself.
And by contact, the Guru indeed makes it gold, equal to himself.

Thus, when the greatness of the Guru has been firmly established in all parts [of the body] and grace has been stabilized in the mind, and when the greatness of the Liṅga has likewise been stabilized, that which follows immediately upon the desire for it to be so is called the "Section on the Greatness of the Liṅga. || 34 ||
In the Sāmaveda.
Within whom all beings abide, and from whom everything proceeds.
That which they call the supreme reality—that is the god Maheśvara.
It has been stated likewise in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
In this, the entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, dissolves.
That from which [the state] arises more abundantly is held to be the supreme *liṅga*. || 36 ||
Furthermore, in the Vīrāgama:
Within the center of the Liṅga is the entire universe, the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving.
There is nothing superior to that which is external to the *liṅga*; therefore, one should worship the *liṅga*.

Thus, for one who has stabilized the majesty of the *liṅga* in the mind and is thus graced, when there arises the desire to know how the majesty of the *jaṅgama* (the embodied deity) abides within knowledge, the subsequent section is called the "Section on the Majestic Power of the *Jaṅgama*" from the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*.

"All this is indeed the Self"—he who sees this, who reflects on this, and who realizes this, finds delight in the Self, sports with the Self, has the Self as his companion, and finds bliss in the Self; he becomes a self-ruler, and for him there is freedom to move at will in all worlds. (Yajurveda 40.7)
The God of gods, the guest. || 40 ||
Furthermore, in the *Ṛgveda*, it is said that when the Lord wandered as a guest, he was intent upon his pursuit.
It has been stated likewise in the Vīrāgama:
The god who is the Supreme Lord exists for the benefit of the entire world.
He moves about in the form of a guest; salutations to you, whose self is the moving world.

Having thus understood the greatness of the Moving One (Jaṅgama) and having accepted his grace, for those who have become happy through that grace and who abide in right conduct, when there arises the inquiry as to how the greatness of the devotee is perceived, the section concerning the "Greatness of the Devotee" (Bhaktamāhātmya) is stated immediately thereafter. || 43 ||
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
Being tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and composed, one sees the Self within the very Self.
Likewise, in the Vīrāgama:
Who indeed knows, in accordance with reality, the greatness of my devotees?
I know it, you know it, and Nandin or Guha knows it as well.
Furthermore, in the Śivadharmottara:
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste (antyaja).
A devotee of Śiva is always worthy of worship, even if he has fallen into any state whatsoever. || 46 ||
In the arrival of the hero.
When a great calamity has befallen him, he should go to the house of a devotee of Śiva.
One should beg for food that is not mixed with meat; if that is not obtained, one should drink water.
Thus, when the greatness of the elements (*bhūta-māhātmya*)— which is non-different from one's own self by virtue of being an object of devotion— is realized as residing within oneself,

and there arises the inquiry as to how the greatness of the supreme bliss of the elements, consisting of transformation and entry into both the external and internal, belongs to the gracious Lord (*prasādinaḥ*), [the following occurs] immediately thereafter.
This is called the section on the majesty of taking refuge. || 48 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
It manifests as the qualities of all the sense organs, yet is devoid of all sense organs.
The Lord and Master of all, the vast refuge of all (or, according to another reading, the Friend).
49 || Likewise, in the *Śivayogapradīpikā*, there is a verse:
Blessed are those cities—free from disease, perpetually festive, and ruled by victorious sovereigns.
Where even a single person, whose self is absorbed in the yoga of Śiva, sanctifies [the place] with his feet by means of his purifying sandals—
in this way, being full of supreme bliss and graciousness in all his limbs— then,
in response to the inquiry as to how the greatness of the grace resulting from his own acceptance [of the world] comes about, [the following occurs] immediately thereafter:
This is called the section on the majesty of serene faith (*prasāda-māhātmya-sthalam*), according to the *Maitreyopaniṣad*.
For by the clarity of the mind, one destroys both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
With a serene self, abiding in the Self, one enjoys imperishable happiness. Furthermore, in the Yajurveda:
The nectar swallowed by Rudra is desired by the gods and others who wish to consume it, and the Vedas also long for it. || 53 ||
Furthermore, in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
He should always consume only the remains of the offerings; he is not a Caṇḍāla, nor is he a Pulkasa. || 54 ||
Likewise, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
When there is serenity, whether one is an insect, a moth, or a human being, [one attains liberation].
Whether a god or even a dānava, one attains supreme knowledge. || 55 ||
In that very place, there is a verse.
There is nothing equal to the grace of Śiva; there is nothing superior to the grace of Śiva.
Through the grace of Śiva comes proximity to Śiva; through the grace of Śiva comes purity of the self. (56)
"Truth, truth, and again truth—raising up my arm, I declare this!"
Through the grace of the Great Lord alone, all attain every accomplishment. || 57 ||

[Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The State of Grace," in the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is a commentary on the *Śrutimālā* of one hundred and one topics, entitled *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*, composed by the venerable Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of Śiva-yogins and wandering ascetic teacher.]
[The Fourth Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva.

Having thus performed the practice of the stage of the devotee (*prasādī*), and having performed it through the gateway of direct experience as one who has become a devotee unified in flavor (*samarasībhūta*) with the serene grace (*prasanna-prasāda*), in response to the inquiry "How does one attain that state of uniform flavor (*sāmarasya*)?", [the following] immediately follows:
It is called the station of Prāṇaliṅgin. || 1 ||

Now, regarding the term *prāṇaliṅga*, does it mean "the liṅga in the vital breath" (expressing a locative sense of support), or "the liṅga of the vital breath" (expressing a genitive sense of relation), or "the vital breath itself is the liṅga" (expressing identity)? Furthermore, whose is this state of being a *prāṇaliṅga*? Moreover, since the word *prāṇa* denotes multiple meanings—just as it does in the case of the word for "lion" (*mṛgendra*)—[the meaning must be determined].
The word *prāṇa* refers to the power of carrying (*vāhika-śakti*) as well as to the *kalās*.

The vital air (prāṇavāyu), consisting of exhalation and inhalation, is a sign of the vital breath (prāṇaliṅga) even when it takes the form of mantra; likewise, the sixfold signs beginning with conduct (ācāra), which operate within the sense organs such as hearing— which are parts of the subtle body— are also signs of the vital breath.

The three circles of the sun, moon, and fire situated within the pericarp of the heart-lotus possess the nature of the *prāṇaliṅga*; likewise, the most subtle *nāda*, which exists as non-different from the mind due to its inseparable connection with them, also possesses the nature of the *prāṇaliṅga*.
If it is argued that the existence of the *prāṇaliṅga* is due to its being non-different from the substrate through the relation of inherence, we say no;
for even the fourfold classification of the aforementioned *prāṇaliṅga* would then be impossible.
For that [object] would result in unreality due to its being within the range of a subtle sense organ. || 3 ||

Furthermore, among the three limbs, the nature of the *liṅga* would be lost in one limb; likewise, even the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) would not cease in that portion of the limb, because the *prāṇaliṅga*—being the very *iṣṭaliṅga* (the desired *liṅga*) that has become the object of one's will—is the focus of meditation. Therefore, it is only the reflection of the desired *liṅga* that falls within the scope of the subtle limb.
It should be understood as the "true liṅga of the vital breath. Likewise, in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
For that very reason, the reflection, anointed within the heart, shines forth as consisting of light and is perfectly pure.
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
Indeed, within the body there is that which is luminous and pure, which ascetics whose defects have been extinguished behold;
thus it is stated in the Vīrāgama.
One should place that linga, held by the living being, into the location of his vital breath.
But he who knows [the distinction] by way of differentiation—neither the mark nor the worship—is [as stated] in that very same [text]: || 7 ||
Having become non-dual with the *iṣṭaliṅga*, one does not perceive the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Just as is the form of reflections in a mirror, so it would be. Again, in that very same place:
The vital breath consists of all reality; Śiva consists of all knowledge.
The union of these two is here called the *prāṇaliṅga*.
Furthermore, in the Śaivaratnākara:
He should be known as a Prāṇaliṅgin once he has realized the impermanence of his former physical form.
Having reflected thus, he constantly contemplated everything within the Liṅga known as Sarvajñāna.

Thus, for one who possesses the connection with the *prāṇaliṅga*—that is, for the "living being" (*liṅgin*) whose very life is the *liṅga*—when there arises the inquiry as to how the sequence of worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* is performed, the "place of worship for the *prāṇaliṅga*" is described immediately thereafter. || 11 ||
In the Atharvaśīrṣa Upaniṣad.
They say that within the vital breaths is the mark of the mind, in which reside anger, thirst, and forbearance.
Having abandoned craving, the root of the web of causes, and having reflected with wisdom, one should then establish oneself in Rudra.
Likewise, it has been stated in the Vātula: || 12 ||
The Prāṇaliṅga, which is perceivable by the mind, is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
"The Śruti says: 'They call that the mark of the mind within the vital breaths. Furthermore, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
The mind is the mark by which one is attached; having reached that [mark], whatever action this person performs here, from those worlds he returns again to this world for the sake of action.
Thus it is for one who desires. But as for one who does not desire—who is free from desire, whose desire is attained, whose desire is the Self—his vital breaths do not depart.
Being Brahman itself, one attains Brahman. Furthermore, in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless, partless Brahman.
That is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self recognize.

Thus, for the *prāṇaliṅgin* who is devoted to the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga* and whose entire sensory apparatus is dissolved into the *liṅga*, when there arises the inquiry as to how the various forms of *liṅgasamādhi* occur, the subsequent section is called the "Stage of Śiva-yoga Samādhi. (Maitreyopaniṣad, Vṛtta).
The bliss that arises when the mind, its impurities shaken off by meditative concentration, is established within the Self.
It cannot be described by speech at all times; it is grasped by oneself through one's own inner organ. || 17 ||
Furthermore, in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad:
Thin like the awn of wild rice, yellow, radiant, and resembling a minute particle.
Within the center of that crest-lock, however, the Supreme Self is established.
Furthermore, in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:
The vital breath is the bow, the self is indeed the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target.
One who is heedful should pierce [the target]; he should become one with the arrow. || 19 ||
Likewise, in the *Yogasāra*:
The individual soul (jīva) is the vibration of the vital breath; it is declared to be the subtle body (liṅga) of the Supreme Self.
The state of oneness of both is proclaimed as samādhi. || 20 ||
Furthermore: "In the inconceivable, primordial source of the universe (sādākhya)."
The all-knowing one, the performer of all actions, the auspicious one who is higher than the highest.
The best of those who know yoga should meditate on the light as being like a spider's thread. || 21 ||
And so it is stated in the Vīrāgama:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the resolution of your question.
And this secret of the self is established within the nature of the mind.
The first station is Ādhāra, and the second is Svādhiṣṭhāna.
The third station is the navel, while the belly is the fourth.
The heart is the fifth location; the throat is declared to be the sixth.
The space between the eyebrows is the seventh place; the eighth is said to be emptiness.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as Śakti, are one Guru, Śiva.
Sadāśiva is the lord of these places in their respective order. || 25 ||
From the substratum arises the performance of duties pertaining to caste, stage of life, and so forth.
Then, through the self-mastery over illusion, addiction, delusion, and so forth, it arises. || 26 ||
From the locus of the navel, there indeed arises the state of tamas, beginning with pride (mada) and so forth.
Phenomena such as hunger and thirst arise from their location within the stomach. || 27 ||
Devotion, peace, compassion, and so forth, which arise from the seat of the heart.
The activities such as speech, power, and detachment originate from the throat. || 28 ||
The activities such as knowledge, wisdom, and power originate from the center between the eyebrows.
Certainty and perpetual bliss arise from abiding in emptiness. || 29 ||
Two of these are the bases of Dharma, and likewise two are the bases of illusion.
The two states of devotion, as well as the two states of detachment. (30)
Saṃsāra arises correctly from the first four locations.
There would indeed be an absence of saṃsāra from the four higher stations. || 31 ||
The first two, the inferior and the middling, are mutually connected.
Likewise, the two upper [stages] are joined as the supreme and the most supreme. || 32 ||
The sixfold group beginning with the *ādisthāna* should be endowed with the seed-syllable of Śakti.
Then, there are two void-places (śūnyasthāna) devoid of the seed-syllable of Śakti; thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Above that, it should be known, is the place called Kailāsanilaya.
That state, known as the Brahma-randhra, is remembered as being without support.

Thus, for one who is established in the samādhi of Śiva-yoga and is a possessor of the prāṇa-liṅga, when there arises the inquiry as to how the innate state (sahajabhāva) of the liṅga situated in the mind in the form of the mental image (manomūrti) occurs, the "Nija-sthala of the Liṅga" is described immediately thereafter in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. 36.
It has been stated likewise in the Sūtasamhitā:
The virtuous Śruti declares that Maheśvara is self-luminous.
And indeed, it has been said: "By its light all this shines. (Verse 37)
Some declare that the supreme knowledge of the Self arising from the Vedānta scriptures is the *liṅga* of Śiva.
Others, moreover, declare that even the knowledge of reality produced by reflection is the characteristic mark of the Supreme.
Other lords of sages, knowers of the Vedas, declare that the linga of Śiva is the Śivalinga.
Since it is not logical for that which is self-luminous [to require another], Śambhu himself is the Liṅga. || 39 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the process of the manifestation of the *liṅga* in every limb occurs for one who possesses innate knowledge and is a *prāṇaliṅgin*, the subsequent section on the *aṅgaliṅga* is now described. (40)

In the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*: "He becomes non-existent indeed if he knows Brahman as non-existent; if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. This is his very self within the body (*śārīra-ātman*). Likewise, in the *Śambhuprabhā*.
That Liṅga which resides within the pure body is my Liṅga, conjoined with the Liṅga.
He by whom that talliṅga is known shall be a possessor of the Aṅgaliṅga. (In that very place).
O beautiful lady, in that Liṅga the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, reside.
He by whom that tall liṅga has been worshipped shall become a possessor of the Aṅgaliṅga.

[Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Section on the Prāṇaliṅga," in the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is an exposition of the *Śrutimālā* consisting of one hundred and one sections, within the *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī* composed by the venerable Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of Paramaśiva yogins and wandering ascetic teacher.]
[The Fifth Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva! Having thus performed the practice at the station of the Prāṇaliṅgin,
with all his limbs merged into the Liṅga, the Prāṇaliṅgin, having practiced by means of right knowledge, [proceeds].
In response to the inquiry, "How is it that difference has become of one flavor? the subsequent state of refuge is described in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
I, seeking liberation, indeed take refuge in that Great God, who is illumined by his own intellect. || 2 ||
Furthermore, in the Praśnopaniṣad:

"I know the Supreme Brahman; there is nothing higher than this. Thus they worshipped him, saying, "You indeed are our father, for you carry us across to the further shore beyond ignorance. Salutations to the Supreme Persons! Salutations to the Supreme Persons! (3) Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
I reflect upon Śiva: by what means has my mind become filled with Śiva?
For one whose body is submerged in milk, no thirst for milk arises. || 4 ||
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha:
Let the winds of the end of the aeon blow, and let the oceans become one.
Let the twelve Ādityas burn; there is no harm for one who is free from mental longing.

Thus, when the one who has taken refuge, having realized his own true nature through great knowledge, has dispelled the darkness that was the object of his own ignorance, the state immediately following this is called the "stage of the dispelling of darkness. (Maitreyopaniṣad 6).

Indeed, this [individual soul] is overcome by the material qualities (guṇas); because of being thus overcome, it falls into a state of delusion, and due to that delusion, it does not perceive the Lord, the Blessed One, who resides within itself as its master and director. Thus it is stated in the Śivadharmottara:
Impurity is said to be ignorance, the cause of the sprout of saṃsāra.
He who is joined with that darkness by means of that [quality] is known as tāmasa.
Furthermore, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Having obtained a guru devoid of knowledge, how could one attain liberation?
Just as one who relies on a shattered boat does not reach the far shore of the ocean. || 9 ||

Thus, having dispelled the darkness that had become the object of knowledge, and having pointed out the excellent knowledge as a refuge, when stability has been attained, it is thereafter called the "place of instruction" (nirdeśasthalam). In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad [it is said]:
"The eternal among the non-eternal, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many."
Those wise ones who perceive Him as abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others. || 11 ||
This, they consider, is the supreme happiness that can be pointed out.
How indeed may I understand that? Does it shine, or does it not shine? || 12 ||
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
