Out of fear, everything in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, was devoured.
He by whom that doubt was consumed—that hero is rare to find on earth. || 13 ||
Furthermore, in the *Yoga-ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
And the Guru is virtuous, wise, and the illuminator of supreme bliss.
One who knows reality and is perfected in reality is the giver of liberation, and no other. Furthermore, in the Yogārṇava, there is a verse:
The fish is intent on bathing; the serpent feeds on air; the ram eats only leaves; the cātaka bird subsists on water alone; and the mouse sleeps every day in its burrow.

"The donkey was indeed intent on smearing himself with ashes, and the crane was devoted to meditation; thus, all austerity centered on knowledge, when devoid of discernment, has become fruitless. (15) In that very same place:
Having abandoned their own abodes, they have taken refuge in the abodes of others.
Living beings go forth out of hope for the acquisition of women, gold, and enjoyments. || 16 ||
Having abandoned the path of worldly beings, he who is united with the Liṅga follows the true path.
He desires and seeks the company of those men who possess the knowledge of Śiva. || 17 ||
Having thus explained right knowledge (*sujñāna*) and understood its own nature,

and having shown that for one who has taken refuge in the all-encompassing limb of the nature of knowledge, great knowledge itself is conduct (*cāritra*) and there is no conduct of bad character apart from it— immediately thereafter:
This is called the locus for the accomplishment of ethical discipline (*śīla*), as stated in the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad.
Him who is difficult to see, who has entered into the secret, who is placed within the cave, who dwells in the abyss, the Ancient One.
Having known the Divine through the attainment of inner yoga, the wise man abandons both joy and sorrow. || 19 ||
The same has been stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.
That which pertains to the desire to know the supreme reality of Śiva.
And detachment from worldly desires is considered that supreme moral conduct. || 20 ||
Furthermore, in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
The vow has Śiva as its sole object, and the eternal observance is likewise fixed upon him.
That by which a person becomes virtuous is called "śīla" by the wise. || 21 ||
Furthermore, in the Laiṅgya [Tantra]:
Śiva alone is the supreme light; nothing else exists.
Thus, they know that which is the state of stability to be the supreme ethical conduct (śīla). || 22 ||

[Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Stage of Seeking Refuge," in the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is a commentary on the *Śrutimālā* of one hundred and one stages, titled *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*, composed by the illustrious Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of Śiva-yogins and wandering ascetic teacher.]

[The Sixth Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva! Thus, having dispelled all doubt through great knowledge in this place of refuge, and having directly realized one's own true nature, one who has found refuge in the nature of supreme bliss— of oneself...

Having forgotten that knowledge and having destroyed even that forgetfulness, when the inquiry arises as to how the distinction [between them] has dissolved into oneness with the Great Liṅga, the "Stage of Oneness" (Aikya-sthala) is described immediately thereafter. || 1 ||
In the Uttaratāpanīya Upaniṣad.

Then, having withdrawn the subtle bodies (liṅgas) and pervaded the three bodies with his splendor, he kindled himself as their substratum; then, having grasped that splendor— the self which is the power of consciousness— and having achieved unity with the qualities (guṇas), [he entered] the great gross and the great subtle.

Having withdrawn the great cause, one should reflect upon it by contemplating the forms of the Hotṛ, the Anujñātṛ, and the Anujñā, according to their respective measures. Furthermore, in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:
Earth is not mine, nor are waters; fire is not mine, nor is wind, and space is not mine either.
Having thus known the form of the Supreme Self, which dwells in the cave of the heart, partless and non-dual;
The witness of all, being pure and devoid of both existence and non-existence, attains the nature of the Supreme Self. || 3 ||
Likewise, it is stated in the Devikālottara:
I am alone; no one belongs to me, nor do I belong to anyone else.
I do not see anyone for whom I do not see him, who belongs to me.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Smṛti]:
Through the yoga of practice, the cognition of all external objects has completely dissolved.
The attainment of the state of Brahman by the individual soul is designated as liberation. || 5 ||
Furthermore, in the Śivādvaita [tradition]:
Strengthened by the self-conceptualization of the Lord as an indivisible and perfect whole.
He who is not deluded by non-difference even in a dream—his oneness is proclaimed here.

Thus, when there is oneness with the Liṅga through absorption in the Great Liṅga (Mahāliṅga), one might ask: "How does the state of being dissolved in all conduct, which is perfected in the six stages (ṣaṭsthala), come about? In response to this inquiry, the "Stage of the Perfection of All Conduct" (Sarvācārasaṃpattisthala) is described immediately hereafter. || 7 ||
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
In the very same way, a person who has a teacher knows this; for him, there is delay only so long as he is not released from the body, and then he shall attain [the Self].
His friends receive the merit of his good deeds, and his enemies receive the demerit of his evil deeds.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so, action does not cling to one who has known the sinless Self.
Likewise, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
Whether walking or standing still, whether waking or even sleeping.
This internal worship, however, consists of all modes of conduct and is perpetual.
Furthermore, in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
He is beautiful with the intense bliss of tasting the supreme nectar of immortality.
Formless, he is solely intent upon the practice and performance of all conduct. || 10 ||
Thus, for one in whom all perfections of conduct are absorbed into every limb through the unity of the *liṅga*, the Great *Liṅga* alone is the vessel;
and that Great *Liṅga* also, having become the vessel for the unity of the *liṅga*, results in the two names dissolving so that their distinction becomes a single vessel.
In response to the inquiry "How so?", it is stated immediately thereafter that [they share] a single vessel. || 11 ||
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
The karmas and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]. || 12 ||
Likewise, in the Sūtrārṇava:
O Lord, for him with whom you have achieved a union of hearts, [all is attained].
He alone is the supreme recipient of all majestic powers and splendors.
Furthermore, in the Śivasūtra:
For the vessel of wisdom is indeed distinguished from external vessels.
Because this [property] would belong to that object, whereas for others it would not be so. || 14 ||

Thus, when the Great Liṅga has been attained, one becomes unified with that Great Liṅga as a single vessel; and when the distinction [between self and Liṅga] has dissolved into the bliss of supreme joy through the state of equanimity (*samarasa*), the subsequent stage called "the place of eating together" is described to answer the inquiry as to how this occurs. || 15 ||
In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
"He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave of the heart in the supreme ether attains all desires together with the wise Brahman. Thus it is likewise stated in the Vātula.
Thus, he who knows in reality that everything is offered to the Liṅga—
That wise one enjoys all desires together with Brahman. || 17 ||
Furthermore, in the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad:
By which one [perceives] form, taste, smell, sounds, and touches through sexual union.
By this very means one knows; what remains here? || 18 ||
It has been stated in exactly that way.
By which [means] one [perceives] odors, tastes, forms, touches, sounds, and the act of pleasure.
By this very [means] one knows; what remains here? || 19 ||
In that very same [text].
Possessing a subtle body (liṅgadeha), he is one with the self of Śiva; he follows the conduct of the liṅga and is not a worldly person.
Everything is said to consist of the Liṅga; together with the Liṅga, he enjoys all things.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Stage of Unity," within the section on "The Exposition of the Limbs" in the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is a commentary on the *Śrutimālā* of one hundred and one stages, composed by the illustrious *Paramaśivayogirāṭ* and wandering ascetic teacher (Parivrājakācārya), Śrī Toṇṭadārya, known as the *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*.
The treatise is completed.
[The First Section of the Second Half] | Salutations to Śrī Śiva. Thus,
for one who has taken refuge in the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala*) characterized by the forty-four subsidiary stations (*aṅgasthala*), within the station of the mind (*manasthala*):
In response to the inquiry as to how the investigation of the stages of stability, the *liṅga*, and the site (*sthala*) proceeds,

the "stage of the initiating preceptor" (*dīkṣā-guru-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter. Within that, first, for the devotee who has taken refuge in the compassion of the preceptor— belonging to the stage of the devotee previously mentioned— the *ācāra-liṅga* (the emblem of conduct) belongs to that very person.

Having first established the threefold nature [of the Guru] in the form of the Linga and the Mobile (jaṅgama) within the section on the limbs (aṅgasthala) itself, he now introduces the six-fold stage of the Linga (liṅgaṣaṭsthala) for the purpose of teaching its divisions.
The very Liṅga of conduct (*ācāra-liṅga*) worshipped by devotees becomes threefold in the form of the Guru-liṅga and the Jaṅgama-liṅga;
furthermore, each of those three again becomes threefold individually. || 1 ||
And thus: the devotee alone,

having contemplated even the threefold Guru as being of the nature of the limbs of renunciation (tyāga), the limbs of enjoyment (bhoga), and the limbs of yoga (yoga), and having joined the threefold liṅga to the threefold limb through the compassion of the threefold Guru, proceeds in due order.
Having ascertained that such a form of the Liṅga is consciousness itself, which is inherently both self-natured and other-natured, and is indeed mobile;

and having realized that this very mobile form is the vital breath (prāṇa), that alone is the mantra, and that the devotee intent on the utterance of that mantra must remain with the sense of "I am the servant of the threefold mobile form. || 2 ||

Now, one might object: previously, in the section concerning "the Linga and the Aṅga," it was stated that Supreme Śiva—when devoid of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as Kuṇḍalinī—is the Linga, whereas it was established that the Self (Ātman) alone, when devoid of limiting adjuncts such as ignorance (avidyā), is the Aṅga;
yet now, with reference to the Lord of Śiva-yogins, [you speak of] his being the Aṅgin.

Since it has been stated that the three *liṅgas* shine forth within his three limbs— which have been purified by the three initiations (*dīkṣā*) such as *kriyā*— it would be contradictory here to describe the single Self as being both the limb (*aṅga*) and the possessor of the limbs (*aṅgin*). || 3 ||

Furthermore, as for the word *aṅga*, does it denote the body, the individual soul (*jīva*), or a state of non-preeminence? Not the first, because since the Self is all-pervading (*vibhu*), it cannot possess parts like material, effect-natured objects. Nor the second, [because] "I" (*am*)...

Because of the statement, "It is called 'going' (gam) because it goes to Brahman, which is pure existence," the third [alternative] is untenable; for there can be no connection between the individual soul (jīva)—which migrates from one body to another and is joined with the principles such as the ego—and the subtle body (liṅga), which transcends all principles. This is so with respect to the action consisting of a connection.

Since both related parties are primary and the self possesses the status of the principal (aṅgin) by virtue of its connection with the three limbs (aṅgas), it is impossible for a single indicative mark (liṅga) to be connected [to both]. If it is argued that the very connection between the indicative mark and the limb is not tenable, [we reply that] in the world, such connections are seen in cases like a beloved woman’s connection with her lover, or water from the ocean’s roar and so forth.
Just as one may be primary while another is secondary despite being equal, so too,

in the relationship between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, the *liṅga* is primary because its connection with respect to that relationship has been operative since beginningless time by way of creation and so forth.

Because it occurs subsequent to initiation (*dīkṣā*), it is secondary; yet, since the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is a constituent part of that [initiation], the connection of that seeker—who is himself a constituent part—with Paraśiva in the form of the *liṅga* also occurs through the three types of initiations and the three types of *liṅgas* as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, it is of three kinds. || 4 ||

In that context, the connection with the desired linga belongs to the very self designated as "the body" (aṅga), which is conditioned by the gross body and serves as the locus for pride regarding birth, family, and so forth.

The connection of the Self, which pervades the subtle body consisting of thirty principles, with the prāṇa-liṅga is the cause for producing the sprout of the body, organs, and so forth, through the differentiation of pure and impure māyā, which serves as the means for both pure and impure experience.

By means of the Great Liṅga, which is one's own innate consciousness free from modification, [one perceives] the Self— which, though itself causeless, exists upon the collyrium that is the cause of the destruction of ignorance and consists of the forms of knowledge and action, and whose causes have been dense and beginningless.

The relationship with Śiva, who is designated as the *liṅga*, is appropriately described as a threefold connection for this self, which is designated as the *aṅga* because its status as the primary member (*aṅgin*) is merely figurative: namely, an inseparable nature, and the supreme connection. || 5 ||
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad.

"He who is not obtained even for hearing by many; whom, though they hear, many do not know—such a teacher as his speaker is found to be skillful, and such a teacher as his knower is found to be skillfully instructed.
Thus it is said in the *Yogasāra*.
The supreme guru is he who bestows the pure initiation of Śambhu.
To him one should offer one's very self; that true guru is worthy of worship and salutation.
Likewise, it is stated in the Svāyambhuva Sūtra:
Having reached his own spiritual guide, his bonds were severed by initiation.
Free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of affliction, he attains union with Śiva.
Furthermore, in the *Sujñānottara-sūtra*:
With his self bound by these principles and joined with all dharmas, [he remains].
It cannot be liberated by any other means, except through initiation whose essence is Śiva.
Furthermore, in the Mataṅgapārameśvara, there is a verse:
For a living being whose impurities have been burnt away by the fire of initiation, one's own true nature attains manifestation through yoga.
Kissed in the region of the heart by the power of the All-pervading Lord, it does not cease through any other man. || 10 ||
Furthermore, in the Svāyambhuva Sūtra:
By this sequential yoga, he has attained the supreme state of absolute isolation.
Because it is empty of beginningless impurity, it does not attain another existence. || 11 ||
Furthermore, in the Vātula-tantra:
That Guru [removes] the three impurities located within the three bodies.
Having consumed the three marks by means of the three initiations, he taught [the doctrine of] the three marks.
The one supreme Liṅga alone is well-established within this body.
It shines forth in every direction, having as its essence name, form, and activity.
The *iṣṭaliṅga* is on the external limb, while the *prāṇaliṅga* is likewise within.
The liṅga of existence is always well-established in this union with the Self.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the distinction regarding the attainment of the nature of awakening occurs through the means of instruction for one who has received the *liṅga* from the initiating guru (*dīkṣā-guru*) for the purpose of such teaching, the "Stage of the Instructional Guru" (*śikṣā-guru-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 15 ||
In the Upaniṣad of the Yajurveda.
Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: "Speak the truth; practice virtue."
Do not neglect your private study of the Veda; do not be negligent regarding prosperity. Be one for whom the mother is a deity.

Be one for whom the ancestors are gods; be one for whom the teacher is a god; be one for whom the guest is a god. Those actions which are blameless should be practiced, and not others. Those which are our own good deeds [should be followed].
Those [six] should be worshipped by you, and not the others. This is the command; this is the instruction. Thus it is stated in the Vīrāgama.
"This is the talliṅga, the moving soul"—thus it was proclaimed many times by the mobile beings.
O sinless one, right awakening and its worship are declared to be the training (śikṣā). || 17 ||
Furthermore, in the Śivādvaita [tradition]:
By which [means], as the prima facie position, the universe is manifested through differentiation.
We praise that Śiva, who is subsumed within the non-dual position as its ultimate conclusion. || 18 ||
In the observation of the moon.
O Sage, there are many gurus who are devoted to the traditional conduct of their families.
But a guru who is devoid of the conduct of his family lineage is difficult to find, even if he is the only one available. || 19 ||
Likewise, in the *Yogaśataka*, there is a verse (*vṛtta*):

Birth would not come about [in this way]; therefore, one must serve the excellent Guru who is like Uḍḍīśa—whose intellect is not struck down by the scriptures on drama, logic, or the Tantras, and who does not possess knowledge of external sciences.

That Guru who remains declaring his own stainless [nature] to the disciple himself, thereby cutting through the doubts within the disciple, is declared blessed; no other is so, for he only bestows his own ignorance. Furthermore, in the *Tantrasāra*:
He is beautiful, fair-faced, pure, easily accessible, and a knower of all tantras.
One who is free from doubt, who has severed all uncertainty, and who is independent is considered a true Guru. || 21 ||

Thus, having attained the nature of the Guru of Discipline (śikṣāguru) characterized by the external signs, and having attained the state of distinction through the cause of being opened to the glance of supreme knowledge, one becomes the Guru of Knowledge (jñānaguru). In response to the inquiry as to how this occurs, the subsequent section on the Guru of Knowledge is now stated. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad)
To him who had approached him as a disciple, whose mind was perfectly tranquil and who was endowed with self-restraint, that wise one [spoke].
He who knows the imperishable, true Person—him he [the teacher] truly taught that knowledge of Brahman. || 23 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Vīrāgama:
The worship of Śiva arises from the latent impressions of virtuous deeds performed in one's own previous births.
Devotion to Śiva itself within one's own mind is known as "one's own experience" (svānubhāva). Likewise, in the Vāsiṣṭha:
And when the darkness of insurmountable doubt is obstructed, [he becomes] the sun of consciousness.
And the Guru is said to be knowledge itself, for he knows the reality of the Self through his own direct experience.
Furthermore, in the Śivadharmottara:
The Guru is said to be the root of knowledge; he is the most excellent initiator.
But through knowledge, one becomes a great adept (mahāsiddha) established in the state of a lord of yogis. || 26 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the very *liṅga* that has become one with the nature of the threefold Guru can attain the state of being the *iṣṭaliṅga* (the chosen *liṅga*) within the limbs of refuge, the stage of the *kriyāliṅga* is described immediately thereafter.
27 || In the Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad ||
Rudra spoke of oneness; indeed, Rudra is eternal and ancient. Through austerity, one attains the desired vigor. Thus it is stated in the Vātula.
The entire great site of the desired liṅga is perceivable by the tip of the range of vision.
It directly brings about the attainment of what is desired and prevents what is undesired. || 29 ||
He always bestows desired strength upon his devotees.
Therefore, the Atharva Veda scripture declares it to be the "chosen liṅga" (iṣṭaliṅga).

Thus, when the state [of consciousness] (*bhāva*), characterized by the practice of the limbs (*aṅga*) and the signs (*liṅga*), has become complete, that which follows is called the stage of the sign of the state (*bhāvaliṅgasthala*). (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad)
That which is graspable through meditative cultivation, known as the Wind, the auspicious one who brings about both existence and non-existence.
Those who know the Lord as the creator of the world-ages have abandoned darkness.
It has been stated likewise in the Vātula.
The partless Bhāvaliṅga is perceivable through internal disposition; it is higher than the highest.
"Pure Being alone is the mark of existence"—this is the firm conclusion of the great-souled ones.
Furthermore, in the Mahābhārata:
The deity does not exist in wood, nor in stone, nor in clay.
But since the deity exists within the state of being (bhāva), therefore one meditates upon him through that state of being.

Thus, when the state of attaining the nature of great knowledge has been reached within the *liṅga* whose form is the true existence full of being (*bhāva*), that which follows is called the stage of the *jñāna-liṅga*. || 35 ||
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
He is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other gods, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action.
Then, with his being purified by the clarity of knowledge, he beholds that partless [reality] while meditating.
Thus it is stated in the Vātula:
That which is declared to be higher than the highest is called the *jñānaliṅga*.
It is beyond cultivation, unmanifest, the supreme Brahman known by the name Śiva.
Furthermore, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
For even those yogins who have renounced all worldly objects do so indeed for the sake of spiritual discipline.
Indeed, having honored the mark of knowledge, they rejoice within their hearts.
Furthermore, in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Satisfaction, characterized by bliss, abides in its state of being free from all limiting conditions.
The sign of knowledge, moreover, is the state of being dense with the bliss arising from that [knowledge], which bestows satisfaction. || 39 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the distinction [between the soul] becomes motionless within the natural quality (*svabhāvaguṇa*) of the refuge— the *liṅga* that has become one with the nature of the threefold *liṅgas*— the "Self-abiding Place" (*svayasthala*) is stated immediately thereafter. (Atharvaśikhopaniṣad).
He conquers even all the words correctly; he himself becomes Brahman, the bringer of perfection. || 41 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Vīrāgama:
Through the thorough knowledge of the mark of the Self, he is Nandī (an alternative reading is Nandīśa, the emblem of Śiva);
having abandoned external ritual acts, he himself is called the Liṅga. 42.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Meditation on Śiva, as well as training and constant adherence to solitude and virtuous conduct.
Since there are four types of karma, a fifth is not possible. || 43 ||
In the Sūtasamhitā:
Having entreated even generous people who are devoted to him for wealth that is very difficult to obtain—
One who is agitated by its absence should never cause agitation [to others].
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
Having honored [it] according to the prescribed rite with a mind fixed on Śiva, out of fear and devotion.
The sage should accept what is given; that alms-food becomes nectar. || 45 ||
In the Śivadharmottara:
One should never accept that very same thing when it is given without faith.
With an undistracted mind and tranquil, one should always recite the auspicious vidyā.
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
He is empty of equality everywhere, yet endowed with equality everywhere.
In this world, one who seeks liberation is praised as being without a useless root or abode.
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Abandoning all undertakings, subsisting on alms-food, and dwelling at the foot of trees.
Freedom from possessiveness, non-malice, and conduct characterized by the application of equanimity. || 48 ||

Thus, when there is the inquiry as to how there can be a distinction in movement while the *liṅga* has become motionless in its own nature by taking devotion as its cause, the "Stage of Movement" (*carasthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 49 ||
In the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad.
Having worn matted hair and being clad in bark garments, he himself wanders through the worlds day after day;
thus it is said in the Ṛgveda.
"Go indeed! Go indeed! For by going, one finds honey. || 51 ||

Furthermore, in the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad: "Clad in a single garment, with a shaven head and an alms-bowl for his belly, he may enter a village for the sake of alms until evening; moving clockwise and free from doubt, he should practice the mendicant's life, avoiding those who are accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their caste. (52)
In the Yajurveda.
Moving through these worlds—the realms of desire and the formless realms—by means of the fire of desire, he remains here singing this Sāman.
It has been stated in the same way in the Vīrāgama:
One whose nature is non-different from the Śiva-liṅga, who has withdrawn the entire collection of his senses into it,
who wanders at will, and whose joy is in himself— he is called a *cara-liṅga*.
Likewise, the conduct [is described] in the Vātula.
Or by the destruction of the unreal cycle of existence through the authority of scripture and the path of reasoning.
As Śiva awakens, he should again move about in his own playful sport, singing of that very [awakening] itself.
Furthermore, in the *Yogasāra*:
He wanders the earth according to his own will, even while enjoying the objects of the senses.
He who is a non-doer within and a doer without is that yogi, the sovereign of royal yoga.
Furthermore, in the Śivayogadīpikā:
Wandering through all fields of merit for the sake of his own livelihood.
When begging from virtuous people, one should never cause distress to those who are impoverished.
Likewise, in the Vātula-tantra:
Just as a bee, even while taking nectar, does not harm the flower.
Likewise, one should receive alms from the master of the house in the manner of the "bee-gathering" (mādhukarī).

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the supreme and the non-supreme emerge from the moving liṅga that has been set in motion for the sake of devotion, the "Supreme Abode" (parasthala) is described immediately thereafter. In the Haṃsa Upaniṣad it is said:
"Clad in space, he offers no salutation, no *svadhā* invocation, no censure, and no praise; he follows whatever comes by chance."

A monk neither invokes nor dismisses, neither recites mantras nor practices meditation; he has no object of worship and no focal point, being neither separate nor non-separate—he is a monk who abides everywhere without a dwelling-place. || 60 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Vīrāgama:
That which is the supreme locus of the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva.
This very stationary linga is declared to be the supreme linga.
Likewise, in the Bhagavadgītā:
He remains silent toward both blame and praise, and is content with whatever comes his way.
He who is homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion—he is dear to me.
Also in the Vātula [Tantra]:
"The Liṅga is Śiva, the body is the Kṣetra, and their union is the substratum."
Therefore, whoever is joined with both the external signs and the internal limbs becomes an *atyāśramin*.
Furthermore, in the Devikālottara:
There is no cause, there is no fruit, and there is no action by way of intrinsic nature.
All this is non-existent; there is neither a world nor anything worldly.
In this, there is no worship, no prostration, no recitation, and no meditation.
It has been stated that the object of knowledge is exclusively [the self]; nothing whatsoever else is to be known. 65.
Furthermore, in the Yogārṇava:
Through pride in one's caste and stage of life, a person becomes a slave to the Veda.
If one free from conceit abides at the pinnacle of the sacred scriptures, || 66 ||
In the Sūtasamhitā:
He for whom the conduct of caste and stage of life has dissolved through the vision of his own Self.
Having transcended all castes and stages of life, he remains established in his own self.
In another tantra:
Having abandoned the fragments of saṃsāra, though possessing all arts (kalāvān), he is partless (niṣkala).
He whose mind is even mindless is called liberated while living.

Thus concludes the *Kaivalya*, titled the *Commentary on the Garland of Scriptural Verses on the One Hundred and One Stages*, composed by the illustrious *Paramaśivayogirāṭ* and wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*) Śrī Toṇṭadārya within the *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*.
In the *Alyasāra*, in the determination of the stages of the *liṅga*, the first chapter, titled "The Stage of the Conduct-liṅga" (*ācāraliṅgasthala*),
is completed.
[The Second Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the unified Liṅga— consisting of the triad of mobile, stationary, and fixed forms— attains its nature as the Āgama within the ritual practice of the Vīramāheśvara, the subsequent stage is called the "Stage of Ritual Practice" (Kriyāgama-sthala). || 1 ||

Then, having correctly taught the nature of the *paripūrṇācāra-liṅga* as the crest-jewel among all mobile and immobile beings, as well as its various sub-divisions, [the text proceeds] thereafter with regard to the Māheśvara who has accomplished his purpose by taking exclusive refuge in the *parajaṅgama*.
In order to demonstrate that the very mobile world, which has become a refuge, is to be worshipped as the ninefold ground for that [Lord] alone,
[the text describes] the form and other qualities of the Māheśvara who is qualified for that, according to the threefold nature of the *āgama-liṅga*.
By being firmly established in the conduct prescribed for the station of Māheśvara, one possesses devotion to the *liṅga*;
there is the comprehension of the threefold nature of the bodily *liṅga*, the rejection of everything from the previous substratum up to the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*),
the rejection of the all-pervasive through the threefold nature of the conduct-*liṅga*, and the realization that Śiva is identical with the universe.

Having established [the deity] in that *liṅga* and having attained the certainty that it is the *bhaktadehika-liṅga*, one should perform the investigation of the ninefold *guruliṅga*. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad).

"Therefore, this is the truth: those rituals which the seers beheld in the mantras, they were extensively propagated in the Tretā age; perform them constantly, O you who desire the Truth—this is your path to the world of the well-done.
Thus it is stated in the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi.
Just as fire does not manifest without the fire-drill and fuel.
Likewise, without ritual action, Śiva, though abiding within, would not become manifest. || 4 ||
In the Rigveda.

"This hand of mine is the Blessed One; this [hand] of mine is the more blessed one. This is my universal medicine; this is the auspicious touch. This is the mother; this is the father; this has come as the restorer of life. This is your crawling forth;
depart from here for the sake of Subandhu. Thus it is likewise stated in the Vātula.
Whoever always holds in his hand Śiva in the form of a liṅga.
Know that my state, the abode of all perfections, is held in his hand.
In the Yajurveda.
May the Maruts be gracious for your glory, O Rudra; may that wondrous and beautiful birth of yours, and that supreme station of Viṣṇu which is established as a treasure, [be ours]. 7.
Likewise, in the Tātparya-saṃgraha, in verse:
Even though he brings auspiciousness through the glory of wealth, you are detached from that prosperity by which you, the Lord of Śrī, have been appointed as his servant;
for her sake, they declare that your birth was of beautiful and manifold form, honored by the Maruts.
(Rigveda)
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant one, the increaser of prosperity.
May I be liberated from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, but not from immortality. || 9 ||
Likewise, in the Laiṅgya [Tantra]:
One should worship the three-eyed God, who is fragrant and the increaser of prosperity.
What can death do to me? For I am likewise the death of death.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the *liṅga*— which has assumed the nature of the *Kriyāgama*— attains the state of being differentiated from the nature of the *Bhāvāgama* of the Great Lord (*Māheśvara*), the subsequent section on the *Bhāvāgama* is now described. (From the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.)
Whatever one worships, in whatever manner, that very thing becomes; it becomes the nature of that which is its state.
As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become. Thus it is said in the Yogārṇava:
Śiva is the form of light, complete, and transcending all universal splendor.
And by meditating on [the deity] who illuminates the intention, one should become absorbed in that. || 13 ||
Also in the Kāmikāgama:
The wise man should meditate incessantly upon the great and most noble Mahāliṅga, which is indescribable, incomparable, and the conqueror of the delusions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. || 14 ||

Having thus become perfected in the culmination, and having attained the distinction of the nature of the scriptural tradition of knowledge (jñānāgama) of Maheśvara— whose signs are present through the existence of the reality of being— the next stage is called the "Section on the Scriptural Tradition of Knowledge" (jñānāgamasthala), in response to the inquiry as to how this occurs. || 15 ||
In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad.
Making the self the lower fire-drill and the syllable Om the upper fire-drill,
Through the practice of churning with knowledge, the wise man burns away the fetter.
And likewise in the Āgneya Purāṇa:
By means of the scriptures, virtuous people, and noble deeds, one should be repeatedly and thoroughly instructed.
The constant attainment of knowledge should always be understood by those who travel the path of knowledge. || 17 ||
And in the Sūtasamhitā:
Reality is free from conceptual construction; it is knowledge, bliss, and non-dual.
Those who see [this] are liberated; even while living, they have no doubt [of this]. || 18 ||
Furthermore, in the Siddhāntarahasya:
Nor should one ever, at any time, be bound by the restrictive rules prescribed in the scriptures.
This worship of Śambhu through knowledge is for those whose minds are undisturbed.
Also in the Śivadharmottara:
Just as darkness is not destroyed by the mere remembrance of light.
Likewise, Śiva cannot be realized through ritual actions and the like when they are devoid of right knowledge.

Thus, having described the threefold nature of the *liṅga* according to the scriptures and the nature of the *liṅga* as unified through the churning of all limbs—which constitutes the connection between the *liṅga* and the body—the next stage, "the state with body" (*sakāyasthala*), is stated in response to the inquiry: "How is it that difference has been attained? || 21 ||
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
If a person were to know the Self as "This am I," [he would realize his true nature].
Desiring what, and for the sake of what desire, would one suffer here in this body?
Furthermore, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad:
Adorning the body with alms-food, clothing, and ornaments, people think, "By this we shall conquer that world. || 23 ||
It has been stated likewise in the *Trikāṇḍasāra*:
If not, then it would be constrained by its effects, such as grossness, and by their attributes as well.
One who practices devotion toward Him while knowing that [the Self] is his own body is called a *sakāya*. || 24 ||
Furthermore, in the *Śambhuprabhā*:
By whichever body Śiva is always maintained in the form of a symbol (liṅga).
He alone, by virtue of that very body, is proclaimed to be "possessed of a body. || 25 ||
Likewise, in the Devikālottara:
He is forever liberated from all dualities and eternally devoid of worldly company.
By means of this very body, he shines forth as the omniscient one.
Also in the Vātula [Tantra]:
Thus, the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) would possess the characteristic of supreme liberation.
Purified by being permeated with that state, his conduct is directly sanctifying. || 27 ||

Thus, in response to the inquiry as to how the state of bodilessness (*nirdehabhāva*) comes about for the devotee of Maheśvara through the churning of the body of the *liṅga*, the "Stage of the Bodiless" (*akāyasthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 28 ||
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

Whether his body, while dwelling here, touches what is dear or not dear to its friends, or whether it is bodiless— just as wind, cloud, lightning, and thunder are bodiless; and just as these, having arisen from that space (ākāśa) and attained the form of the supreme light, [merge] by their own...
He is manifested through form. Furthermore, in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad:
By many Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas.
For me there is neither merit nor sin, nor destruction, nor birth; nor even body, senses, or intellects.
It has been stated likewise in the Skanda Purāṇa:
With extremely firm devotion, consisting of a single-minded absorption in the reality of Śiva.
One who has abandoned attachment to the body and so forth is proclaimed as "without body" (akāya). || 31 ||
Furthermore, in the Śaivaratnākara:
That desired liṅga is the abode of the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness.
He whose body is dissolved here in this Linga becomes bodiless; he shall become great. || 32 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the distinction between the embodied (sakala), the unembodied (niṣkala), and that which transcends the body (atītakāya) pertains to the *liṅga* that has attained the nature of being bodiless, the subsequent section concerning "another's body" (*parakāyasthala*) is stated. || 33 ||
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
Whatever may be the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the act of enjoying within the three abodes;
Distinct from them, I am the witness, pure consciousness alone, the eternally auspicious Śiva.
It has been stated likewise in the Vātula.
That which is to be enjoyed and the enjoyer proclaimed in the three abodes—
He who knows both, while enjoying, is not defiled. || 35 ||
Likewise, in the Svāyambhuva Sūtra:
For this enjoyer of worldly experiences who has been offered unto the abode of Śiva, there is never [any such thing].
The state of being an enjoyer, the state of being an authority, and the imitation of the original form. || 36 ||
Furthermore, in the Āditya Purāṇa:
All the lords of the Gaṇas assume forms at will and act according to their own desire.
Having enjoyed pleasures together with Śiva, they go to the state of Śiva. || 37 ||
In the Śaivaratnākara.
His physical body is the sprout of the seed of saṃsāra, consumed by the fire of consciousness.
And he who has taken up the external limb (parāṅga) with the subtle liṅga as his support is one whose conduct is such. || 38 ||

Thus, regarding the threefold nature of the bodily signs (kāyaliṅga) and the unified sign (ekībhūtaliṅga) for the sake of the practice of the true dharma of the Great Lord (Māheśvara), the stage of the practice of dharma (dharmācārasthala) is stated immediately following the inquiry as to how the distinction between them becomes unified. || 39 ||
In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.

Dharma is the foundation of the entire world; in this world, subjects approach the most righteous person; by means of dharma one dispels evil; everything is established in dharma; therefore, they say that dharma is supreme. || 40 ||
In the Vātula [Tantra].
The non-abandonment of right conduct, which has been well-adopted with devotion.
Even at the risk of one's life, this is called the practice of dharma. || 41 ||
Furthermore, in the Āditya Purāṇa:
Dharma has been declared to be of many kinds by the sages who perceive the truth.
Therein lies the supreme, inexhaustible, eternal Dharma, the Śiva-dharma.
Also in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
One should constantly worship Śiva with pure dharma.
One attains the state of Śiva, which is supreme bliss and imperishable. || 43 ||
In the Devikālottara.
And likewise, O Goddess, [he consumes] worms, insects, moths, and trees.
A wise person, whose mind is fixed on the ultimate truth, should not destroy living beings. || 44 ||
In exactly the same way.
One should not uproot the roots, and one should avoid cutting the leaves.
One should not cause affliction to living beings, nor should one pluck flowers.
The worship of Śiva should be performed with flowers that have fallen of their own accord. || 45 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the characteristic mark (liṅga) consisting of the very nature of the practice of dharma becomes firmly established in the sphere of the mind of a devotee of Maheśvara through conduct rooted in true being, the "stage of the practice of inner disposition" (bhāvācārasthala) is described immediately thereafter. || 46 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: [The] Metre.
He who employs all beings and all constituent elements, as well as actions endowed with qualities, [is the Supreme Lord].
In the absence of these [elements], there is the destruction of performed actions; upon the exhaustion of karma, he goes to that which is truly other. || 47 ||
Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Even for those who perform ritual actions, even while they are constantly performing virtuous deeds.
All ritual actions would be deficient without unwavering contemplation. (48)
Also in the Laiṅgya:
But purity of being is indeed purity; therefore, one should follow their conduct in its entirety.
The wise one should meditate incessantly with a state of being that is indeed pure. || 49 ||
In the Vātula [Tantra].
One should not practice the non-duality of action; one should practice the non-duality of being.
But that action which is carried out with purity of intention, O Śāṅkarī, [is truly effective]. 50.
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
It lasts for the duration of milking a cow, or the distance of an arrow's flight, or merely the blink of an eye.
One who is once joined to the supreme state shall not undergo rebirth again. || 51 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the external *liṅga* associated with the true state and conduct of Maheśvara— which exists within the mind— is distinct from [the internal state] attained through great knowledge and conduct, the "Stage of the Conduct of Knowledge" (*jñānācāra-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)
He is the witness to the truth of the self, the embodiment of existence, and possessed of great majesty.
He for whom the self is dear does not commit evil deeds. || 53 ||
In that very same place.
For one who perceives all beings correctly as being the self of all beings.
For even the gods are deluded regarding the path, though they seek the goal by means of footprints, due to their knowledge of those very footprints.
It has been stated exactly so in the Kāmikāgama.
The supreme reality is beyond knowledge, absolute, and facing in all directions.
One should, however, contemplate the nature of the absolute Self in the form of pure consciousness. || 55 ||
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
Thus, the steadfast one, having taken refuge in rest within that supreme, pure reality.
Even while engaging in external and internal activities, he relishes that very [state] within.
Furthermore, in the Sarvajñānottara:
And he who views all things with equanimity is liberated from all bonds.
Everything shines as consisting of Śiva; nothing inauspicious exists anywhere. || 57 ||
Likewise, in the Devikālottara:
The body consists of the five elements, and Śiva resides right there within it.
This world, from Śiva down to the earth, is of the nature of Śaṅkara.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Stage of the Guru-Liṅga," within the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is a commentary on the *Śrutimālā* of one hundred and one stages, composed by the venerable Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of yogis of Śiva and wandering ascetic teacher, in this work known as the *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*.
[Completed] ||
[The Third Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva. Thus, having established the threefold nature of the *ācāraliṅga* and the *ekībhūtaliṅga*,
and regarding the question of how the distinction is internalized within the body of one who has attained grace through the *liṅga*, immediately thereafter—
It is called the place of bodily support. || 1 ||

Now, when the stage of the threefold *ācāra-liṅga* of the distinguished Māheśvara—characterized by devotion, the body, and the *kaliṅga*—is thoroughly investigated with mindfulness, that very thing becomes the *guru-liṅga*. Through the perfection of right conduct (*sadācāra*), that very thing becomes the *śiva-liṅga*. In that very *śiva-liṅga*...

When [the state of] being one who enjoys [all things] having offered them all [to the Lord] is itself grace (*prasāda*), then— within that threefold classification of *anugraha-liṅga*— having become uninterrupted, one traverses from the greatness of the Guru up to the greatness of the refuge; then, within the threefold classification of *arpita-liṅga*, being of that very nature, one personally becomes the greatness of grace itself, [and likewise] within the threefold classification of *tanu-karaṇa-liṅga*.
By beholding one's own true nature, the attainment of grace is achieved solely through constant attentiveness toward the Śivaliṅga. || 2 ||
In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad, the meter is Vṛtta.
And being pure, seated on a comfortable seat in a secluded place, with his neck, head, and body held straight;
Abiding in the state beyond all stages of life (atyāśrama), having restrained all the senses and bowed with devotion to his own guru, || 3 ||
Likewise, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
Just as a worm, through the contemplation of being a bee, is born as one just like it.
By application to the state of Śiva, a person becomes exactly like that. || 4 ||
And in the Yogadīpikā:
Just as one becomes a Brahmin through the perfection of ritual refinement, so does one attain the status of the twice-born.
Likewise, through the perfection of such instruction, even a man may become extraordinary.
Likewise, in the Śivarahasya:
The body of one bitten by a serpent is that very same body as if it were a body of poison.
Whatever body belongs to one who has been bitten by a *liṅga* [snake], that body becomes like the body of a *liṅga*.
In that very same [text].
Cotton combined with oil becomes like fire through contact with light; likewise, a true devotee endowed with devotion becomes like the Liṅga through contact with the Liṅga.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the differentiation of the elements— which have become connected to the pleasure of all the senses— occurs in one whose *liṅga* is grasped by a body endowed with such clarity, the "Stage of the Favoring of the Senses" (*indriyānugraha-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 8 ||
In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
Having held the body perfectly straight with the three parts elevated, and having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind;
The wise man should cross over all terrifying currents by means of the raft of Brahman.
In the non-duality of Śiva.
The outward-turned sense faculties give rise to the emergence of existence.
When turned inward, those very same [faculties] become the causes for the destruction of saṃsāra. || 10 ||
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the senses, and the three qualities.
Indeed, no transformations whatsoever affect that great-souled one.
In the Bhagavadgītā.
Moving among sense objects with the senses free from passion and hatred.
One who has mastered the self attains tranquility through the senses that are under one's own control. || 12 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the distinction of the stage of the *prāṇaliṅga*— in which the serene vital breath (*prāṇa*) is embraced by the sign (*liṅga*) consisting of the connection with all the senses—
is established, the "stage of the favoring of the vital breath" (*prāṇānugrahasthala*) is described immediately thereafter in the Kauśītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad.

That which is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa) is wisdom (prajñā), and that which is wisdom is the vital breath; these two dwell together in this body and depart together from it. Thus it is stated in the Candrāvalokana.
Wherever the mind finds stability upon seeing it, and wherever indeed the vital breath (māruta) abides;
If he should thus become despondent in some way, this [practice] shall be his grace. || 15 ||
Furthermore, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Just as iron attains the state of gold through the application of medicinal herbs.
Likewise, through meditation on the Self, the vital breath (prāṇa) attains the state of the Supreme Self.

Thus, having described the threefold nature of the *anugraha-liṅga* (the sign of grace), the *ekībhūta-liṅga* (the unified sign), and the *liṅgaprasādin* (the one who has attained the grace of the sign)— namely, the distinction between those who have offered their faces and those who have become the *liṅga* itself— the next stage, "offering the body" (*kāyārpaṇa-sthala*), is stated in response to the inquiry as to how [this occurs]. [This is found] in the *Praśnopaniṣad*.
Now, just as there is happiness in this body— just as, my dear, birds settle upon a banyan tree, even so indeed does all that settle in the supreme Self. Thus it has been stated in the Śivarahasya.
When the yogi offers his own body to Śiva, [he attains liberation].
Then it becomes that very form, the form of Śiva; of this there is no doubt. || 19 ||
Furthermore, in the Bṛhatkālottara:
In unions and in separations, there are pleasures no larger than an atom.
Whoever should perform [this] constantly and with vigilance at the desired liṅga, || 20 ||
Likewise, in the Yogajagama:
When he offered his own self to Śiva, who is the soul of the Guru;
Then, O Goddess, one becomes a Śaiva; from that state, there is no further rebirth. || 21 ||
Furthermore, in the Śivayogadīpikā:
And those spectacles which provide delight to the eye.
Having accomplished these with his body, he should always offer them to Śiva.

Thus, when the *liṅga* has its face directed toward the body, it is for one who is serene; when its face is directed toward the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it is for one who has attained distinction.
To address the inquiry as to how this occurs, the subsequent stage of "the face directed toward the instruments" (*karaṇārpita*) is described.
(Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad).
But he who possesses discernment and is endowed with a disciplined mind—
His senses are under his control, like well-trained horses are under the control of a charioteer.
In that very same [text].
Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself.
Know the intellect to be the charioteer, and the mind indeed to be the reins. || 25 ||
They say the senses are the horses, and the objects of the senses are their paths.
The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer. || 26 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Śivarahasya:
That by which the entire internal organ is made to turn inward toward Śiva;
He whose internal organ (mind) has been offered [to the Lord] is called one who offers his instruments. || 27 ||
In the Śaivaratnākara.
Whatever pleasure has entered the senses, let that be offered to Śiva.
And that grace should be enjoyed through the medium of those very senses.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā].
Thus detached, he should offer that very thing with his own mind.
Seeing, touching, smelling, eating, hearing, and so forth. || 29 ||

Thus, when the bliss offered within the internal organ has reached the subtle body (*liṅga*) and [the soul] is serene, how is it that the state of being entirely offered and having attained non-difference occurs spontaneously in all limbs? To satisfy this inquiry, the "Stage of Offering through Contemplation" (*bhāvārpitasthala*) is described immediately thereafter in the *Maitreyopaniṣad*.
Having made the mind perfectly steady, free from both lethargy and distraction.
When one attains the state of *unmanī* within the self, then that is the supreme state.
Likewise, in the Śivarahasya:
Wherein there may be the state of being for the supreme self, Śiva.
That which is offered first as the foremost is intended to be an offering made with devotion.
In that very same [text].
He whose mind contemplates the flood of objects established in the consciousness.
That state of mind which is offered up—O Śiva—that would be the "offerer of the state" (bhāvārpaka).
Furthermore, in the Rudrayāmala:
Because his state was surrendered to the Lord, he was free from the occurrences of association with loved ones.
The wise man should be only slightly touched by the transformations of nature and should remain endowed with pure being.
Likewise, in the Vāsiṣṭha:
"Contemplating the association with the group of beloved ones as being indeed auspicious."
By abandoning the ego-sense, one attains the purification of existence. || 35 ||
Furthermore, in the *Vimarśanasāhasrī*:
The state that bestows [liberation] upon all—place that state within the supreme Śiva.
For one who has correctly surrendered [everything], what else remains? || 36 ||
In the Vātula [Tantra].
The entire body shall be the linga itself; food, drink, and so forth are offered [to it].
Faith itself shall be satisfaction; everything shall become composed of the Liṅga. || 37 ||
In that very [Brahman] are the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the one who causes enjoyment—all this, both moving and unmoving.
By meditating upon it as having the form of Śiva, one becomes Śiva in reality. || 38 ||

Thus, when the threefold stage of the *arpita-liṅga* has become unified within the gracious (*prasādini*) [state], and the distinction regarding the state of being a disciple has been attained through the means of instruction, the "stage of the disciple" (*śiṣya-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter to address the inquiry as to how this occurs. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad).
Having attained this, the sages— satisfied with knowledge, perfected in self, free from passion, and tranquil—
having reached that which is all-pervading and omnipresent, those wise ones, with disciplined minds, enter into the All itself.
Likewise, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
For those who do not fall into despondency, even when dragged away or beaten;
They are the fit and self-controlled disciples for the rite of Śiva-consecration.
In the non-duality of Śiva,
having attained a state of humble devotion through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
He who always possesses devotion to the guru is called a disciple. || 42 ||
In that very same [text].
They are upright, gentle, pure, disciplined, and firm-minded.
Disciples endowed with purity and proper conduct are proclaimed here. || 43 ||
In the *Śambhuprabhā*.
Having approached the tranquil Guru, who is an ocean of the nectar of Śiva-knowledge,
But he who constantly devotes himself [to this] is called a disciple. || 44 ||

Thus, when the *liṅga* has entered the state of a disciple and has attained a sense of service toward the body of the gracious one (*prasādina*), the stage of service (*śuśrūṣā-sthala*) is described immediately thereafter to address the inquiry as to how that differentiation is achieved.
45 || In the Praśnopaniṣad ||
Endowed there with austerity, celibacy, and faith, he experiences greatness. || 46 ||
Furthermore, in the Kenopaniṣad:
One should serve the teacher until the end of one's conditioned existence. Furthermore, in the Pārāśara-śruti:
Therefore, among sons, one who is intent on service is the most beloved; he becomes the closest, the very closest to Brahman. Thus it has been stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Service to the guru must be performed, as well as compliance with the guru’s word.
Always devoted to the guru, one should never transgress the guru’s command. || 49 ||
Furthermore, in the Sūtasamhitā:
Of the supreme yogin who is established in the realization of supreme non-duality.
Service is indeed the means for attaining pure knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
In the Mānava Purāṇa:
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Therefore, the service of the guru should be performed with body, mind, and speech. (51)
In the Yajurveda.

Having brought dear wealth to the teacher, [the practitioner]— whose outward signs have thus become imbued with the spirit of service— attains a state of identity between teacher and disciple free from mutual superimposition, wherein distinctions have vanished within the body of the gracious one.
In response to the inquiry "How so?", the subsequent [verse] states: "The place to be resorted to. (52)
In the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
The knot of the heart is rent asunder, and all doubts are cut away.
And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
It has been stated likewise in the Vātula.
When that supreme sign (liṅga) is seen—partless and free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika)—
Indeed, all the karmas of this living being are completely exhausted.
And the knot at the heart of ignorance is split asunder in a hundred ways.
Doubts and manifold conceptual constructions are severed in a thousand ways.
In another treatise:
Śiva does not appear through means; rather, those means shine by His grace.
I am that very one, self-luminous, shining as the illuminator of the universe.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Stage of the Śiva-liṅga," within the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is a commentary on the *Ekottaraśatasthalashrutimālā* entitled *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*, composed by the illustrious Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of yogis of Paramaśiva and wandering ascetic teacher.
[Completed] ||
[The Fourth Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva! Thus, having established the threefold nature of the subtle, quality-based, and symbol-based *liṅgas* as the unified *liṅga*,

and having brought about the cessation of the state of being a living soul (*jīva-bhāva*) within the one who possesses the *prāṇaliṅga*, [one attains] the perfection of the *liṅga* and the living soul.
In response to the inquiry as to how the distinction [between the Lord and the self] is attained, the subsequent section concerning the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is stated. Now,

having become a devotee toward the three forms of the Lord who is thus gracious, and perceiving that within the *jaṅgama-liṅga*— the mobile form of His devotees— the very essence is consciousness, one should [worship] in that *jaṅgama-liṅga*.

Through the devotion of direct experience, having become a *prāṇaliṅgin* whose vital breath has become one with the state of equanimity (*samarasa*), and by means of the threefold nature of the *ātman-liṅga*, becoming a worshipper of the *prāṇaliṅga*; and having attained the *samādhi* of Śiva-yoga,
having contemplated the *liṅga* as his own self through the threefold nature of the *nirupaliṅga*, [he remains] by means of that *liṅga* which is his own.
Having remained within the threefold classification of *prasādaliṅga* and understood that very *prasādaliṅga* to be the limb (*aṅga*),
he attained a state of essential oneness (*samarasatva*) within the threefold classification of *pādodakaliṅga*, thereby reaching the nature of a *prāṇaliṅgin*. (Vṛddhajābālopaniṣad)
The nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of being possessed of all blemishes, birth, suffering, and so forth;

egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is the ignorance of that [true nature]. Possessed by that [egoism], the soul becomes an enjoyer of heaven and hell, submerged in the ocean of *saṃsāra*, characterized by false conceit, and once again a locus of sin.
It arises again. Furthermore, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:
"Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, divided a hundredfold..."
That living soul (jīva) is to be known as a portion; and it is destined for infinity.
It has been stated exactly so in the Svāyambhuva-sūtra.
Consciousness intensified by *kalā*, with its objects revealed by *vidyā*.
And being colored by passion, he is also joined with the instruments of cognition and the rest.
From Māyā down to the earth, on the path consisting of the principles (tattva), the elements (bhūta), and the self (ātman).
Remaining there, the person, whose sole delight is in enjoyment, experiences pleasures.
In the Kiranagama.
Due to the connection with beginningless impurity, I have been described as possessing some degree of ignorance.
Because he is free from beginningless impurity, he is omniscient; therefore, he is Śiva.
In another treatise:
The individual soul is Śiva, and Śiva is the individual soul; the living being is truly Śiva alone.
Bound by the noose is the individual soul (jīva); freed from the noose is Sadāśiva.
Furthermore, elsewhere it says:
He who should utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa"—the one named Haṃsa is indeed Sadāśiva.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how one who has attained the discrimination of the Self from the vital breath—which is the sign that turns back the notion of being a living soul—can proceed, the subsequent stage is called the "Inner Self" (antarātma-sthala). || 10 ||
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad.
Just as fire, though one, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form.
In this same way, the single inner self of all beings became the counterpart of every form.
Furthermore, in the Brahmopaniṣad:
The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings.
The supervisor of karma, the abode of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities. 12.
The same has been stated likewise in the Sūtasamhitā.
In that Maheśvara, this entire universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving [is contained].
Through internal reflection, they appear within the graspable Sūtra like a multitude of jewels.
In another treatise:
Even while existing in the present, a person is not joined with the qualities that constitute real entities.
By means of sorrow, joy, fear, anger, greed, delusion, longing, and so forth. || 14 ||
Furthermore, in the Śivasūtra:
Moving through all forms due to its association with the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka).
The inner self is to be known as the stage upon which the Supreme Self dances. || 15 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the distinction remains— despite the *liṅga* having attained the nature of the inner self (*antarātman*) for those who possess the *prāṇaliṅga*, and the supreme self (*paramātman*) abiding while enveloping the nature of discernment (*viveka*)— the "Stage of the Supreme Self" (*paramātmasthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 16 ||
In the Vṛddhajābāla Upaniṣad.

Within the small space (daharākāśa), upon a lotus adorned with a thousand petals and a pericarp embraced by shimmering filaments, the Supreme Self— free from attachment, the witness of all actions, and resembling a lamp in a windless place— abides within the spheres of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. Furthermore, in the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad:
The small, stainless lotus situated in the middle of the city, which has become the dwelling place of another.
Therein also is a small space; free from sorrow, one should worship that which is within it. || 18 ||
It has been stated likewise in another treatise.
For that which has been thoroughly understood, there is indeed neither form nor conceptual construction.
He is the eternal Supreme Self, pervading all beings. || 19 ||
Even when wind and other elements have come into contact with the limbs, there is no experience of touch or the like [without the body].
The form of the living consciousness is that very form of the Supreme Self.
This Self is absolute, self-abiding, peaceful, subtle, and eternal.
There exists within all things the Witness, pure consciousness alone, beyond darkness.
In the Vātula [Tantra].
He sees that body, yet he does not see that [self-]body.
Another person sees those two, yet they both do not see him.

Thus, having explained the threefold nature of the self’s marks, the unified mark, and the conduct of one whose nature is bodiless (*nirdeha*), the subsequent section on the scripture concerning the bodiless (*nirdehāgama*) is now stated, in response to the inquiry as to how one attains such distinction. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)

This Self is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true, and whose resolves are true. (24) Likewise, in the Siddhāntarahasya:
Whatever beings exist upon the earth that are devoted to the tongue and the genitals, [they all perish].
Having renounced the tongue and the generative organ, he is bodiless; he is Maheśvara. || 25 ||
Likewise, in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
That man who makes his own body the equipment for the worship of Śiva.
In a very short time, that man becomes bodiless (videha). || 26 ||
Furthermore, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
That is the fruit of attaining a body, by which one, having served Śaṅkara, [attains that result].
Nor again shall the embodied soul undergo connection with a body. || 27 ||
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Śikṣā]:
Performing actions with the internal senses free from latent impressions (vāsanā).
It does not undergo transformation even by hundreds of disturbances of existence.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how one who has attained the state of distinction— having become a bearer of the *liṅga* through conduct devoid of the body (*nirdeha-cāritrin*)— attains conduct devoid of emotional attachment (*nirbhāva-cāritra*) within the possessor of the *prāṇaliṅga*, the subsequent section on the scripture of the state devoid of emotional attachment (*nirbhāvāgamasthala*) is stated.
(Maitreyopaniṣad)
Just as a fire without fuel subsides by itself.
Likewise, through the destruction of its substrate, the mental state subsides within its own source. || 30 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Vāsiṣṭha:
When no entity is cultivated with regard to any object whatsoever in the world,
Likewise, how can the mind arise within the empty space of the heart? || 31 ||
In that very same [text].
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies here in these three worlds.
And yet, the existence of the modifications of being is not found anywhere. || 32 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the external sign (liṅga) associated with conduct devoid of [true] realization becomes dissolved into the conduct of the one who possesses the vital sign (prāṇaliṅgin), and how one attains freedom from the scriptures and the state of difference— immediately following that, the "Stage of the Destroyed Scripture" (naṣṭāgamasthala) is described. || 33 ||
In the Maitreyopaniṣad.
The mind should be restrained within the heart until it has reached its dissolution.
This is both knowledge and liberation; all other extensive treatises are merely verbal elaborations.
It has been stated exactly thus in the Śivarahasya.
Furthermore, the possibility of rebirth does not exist here for one who is liberated.
Just as no sprouting is seen here from a burnt seed. || 35 ||
Likewise, in the Yogajagama:
Inaction itself is the supreme worship; silence alone is the supreme recitation.
Non-thinking alone is the supreme meditation; desirelessness alone is the supreme fruit.
In that very place: the meter.
Yoga, sleep, sacrifices, conduct, sitting at will, and the great offering to the Deity—these are [the requisites].
Offering as play, giving what is pure to the gods, chanting as idle chatter, sleeping as prostration. (37)
Again, in that very same place:
Action is service; movement is pilgrimage; thought is contemplation; and speech is praise.
Oh, how the worship of Śambhu by the wise is performed with their whole being in every way! 38.
In the Śivarahasya:
Whatever movement arises and occurs for the yogis of Śiva, [it is all for the sake of the world].
That indeed is the worship of the Lord for those whose souls are always absorbed in Him. || 39 ||
In another treatise:
In the fourth state (turya), however, there is the supreme condition (parāvasthā); in that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta), there is the state beyond all beings (nirjanā).
That [consciousness] is lost when the seer and the seen are lost, just as in the case of the lost and the imperceptible.
Furthermore, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
Knowledge of the Brahman of sound is the practice of the Brahman beyond sound; this is the final goal.
That which was called the Brahman of Sound, that same Brahman of Silence moves in silence.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the threefold nature of the *nirupaliṅga* becomes unified with the *liṅgin*— the possessor of the *liṅga*— and attains the state of being of the nature of bliss and serenity, the subsequent stage is called the "Stage of Initial Serenity" (*ādiprasādisthala*). || 42 ||
In the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad.

When the movement of all the senses ceases and one abides in the Self alone, thinking "I am that True Brahman, which is perfect bliss and pure consciousness," one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 43 ||
In the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad, the meter is Vṛtta.
Smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being.
Free from sorrow, he beholds that Lord of unswerving resolve, the Greatness, through the clarity of his own nature. 44.
It has been stated exactly thus in the Śivarahasya:
From tasting the nectar of the guru’s words, which is the cause for the end of rebirth.
He who attains bliss is called one who has attained serenity. || 45 ||
In the Śaivaratnākara.
Through the connection with the state of Śiva, he is called "gracious" (prasādī).
He whose mind has ceased from all things, even toward those who are dear to him. || 46 ||
In another text:
By the power of those sense-faculties whose objects are extremely renowned...
One who is serene through the state of Śiva is celebrated as "prasādin" (the one who bestows grace). || 47 ||
Furthermore, it is also stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Through a supreme application of meditative cultivation, Maheśvara becomes propitiated.
Therefore, his state of being Śiva is called "grace" (prasāda). || 48 ||
In the Vātula [Tantra].
All the activities of this self exist as being projected upon the subtle body (liṅga).
It attains within itself, by itself, that repose characterized by bliss.

When there arises the inquiry as to how the distinction is attained— wherein the *liṅga* has assumed the nature of primordial grace (*prasāda*) and the possessor of the *prāṇaliṅga* has attained the nature of the grace of the vital breath— the subsequent stage of "final grace" (*antya-prasāda*) is now described.
50 || In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad ||
Having realized that "I am that Brahman which illumines the phenomenal world of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth," one is liberated from all bonds. (51)
It has been stated exactly so in the Vātula.
Always, in all states such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
By enjoying what has been offered to the Liṅga, he remains untainted; of this there is no doubt. || 52 ||
In the non-duality of Śiva.
Consciousness itself is the supreme satisfaction, radiant as far as the limits of all objective existence.
In the same way, he who is satisfied with that alone is called one whose faith is ultimate. || 53 ||
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
For one whose own mind has attained the state of pure consciousness alone and has crossed over death.
By what could that supreme bliss which exists be compared?

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the *liṅga*—which has attained the nature of ultimate grace—attains satisfaction within the possessor of the *prāṇaliṅga* once their distinction [from it] has vanished, the subsequent stage called "the state of one who is graced by the object of service" (*sevyaprasādī*) is described. || 55 ||
In the Maitreyopaniṣad.

Then, he said: "That serene being who, having risen up from this body and having reached the supreme light, appears in his own true form—this is the Self; this is the immortal, this is the fearless, this is Brahman."
In the Śivasūtra.
Satisfaction is the dissolution of contraction through the state of fullness of the Supreme Self.
In that very way, one should be satisfied again and again; [this satisfaction] cannot be attained by the tasting of nectar and the like.
In the non-duality of Śiva.
For one satiated by the nectar of knowledge, what is the use of other heaps of food?
Knowledge alone reveals the supreme bliss of Śiva.
Furthermore, in the Śivadharmottara:
For the yogi who has attained fulfillment through the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done.
There is nothing at all that remains to be done; if there were, one would not be a knower of reality.
In the Śaivaratnākara.
For one who is satiated by the nectar of knowledge and whose self is rendered helpless by devotion.
There is never any task to be done, either internally or externally, through contentment.
Also in the Jñānottara:
This [Self] does not exist within the body alone, nor is it situated outside it.
This great joy and serenity shines forth everywhere.
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
Satisfaction, characterized by bliss, abides in a state free from all limiting conditions.
The state of being thick with the bliss arising from that is declared to be the nectar of knowledge.
In the *Tattvasāra*:
O Six-faced One, they are liberated in the aggregate, liberated in the word, and liberated in the form.
But those who are liberated beyond form are truly liberated and have attained contentment. || 63 ||

Thus, having described the threefold nature of the *prasāda-liṅga* as the unified *liṅga* for the *prāṇaliṅgin*s, and in response to the inquiry as to how the state of the *pādodaka*— which has attained differentiation for the purpose of removing the three impurities (*mala*)— is realized, the section on the *dīkṣā-pādodaka* is now stated.
In the Aitareya Upaniṣad.

Now, regarding knowledge (*adhividyā*): the teacher is the prior form, the pupil is the subsequent form; the connection of knowledge is the connection of the oral instruction. (Thus it is stated) in the *Ṛgveda*.
Where shall one proclaim the ford of the Ātman, by which path they drink of the pressed [Soma]?
There are fifteen hymns in a thousand ways; as vast as heaven and earth, so great is this.
A thousandfold are the glories; as far as Brahman is established, so far extends Speech. Thus it has been said.
In the Śivarahasya:
That bliss which is beyond the highest, consisting of the undivided taste of nectar.
For embodied beings, the direct initiation and the water from his feet are indeed difficult to obtain.
In the Yogaśāstra.
He who is purified by the stainless essence of the firmly established true being of Śiva.
Having become purified by another [means], what further need has he for ritual actions and the like? (68)
Furthermore, in the Śivarahasya:
It is the drying up of the mire of evil and the kindling of the fire of wisdom.
The water from the feet of the Guru is wondrous; it destroys the tree of saṃsāra.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how one who has attained a state of distinction—having perceived the true nature of the water from the feet (*pādodaka*) within the reality of the Guru of Instruction (*śikṣāguru*)—is characterized by the *liṅga* that has assumed the very form of the water from the feet of initiation (*dīkṣā*), the subsequent section concerning the water from the feet of Instruction (*śikṣāpādodaka*) is now stated. (In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad: [70]

The sacred foot, spread out, ancient— purified by which one crosses over evil deeds— by that pure, sanctifying foot, being purified, may we cross over sin and the enemy. It is the further shore, the hearing of the world, the radiant door, the sacred, luminous, shining, and greatly-savoring stream of immortality.
May he grant the well-placed [state] to one who beholds his foot being milked in many ways. Thus it is stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
For the destruction of the root of ignorance and for the cessation of birth and karma.
For the sake of attaining knowledge and dispassion, one should drink the water from the feet of the Guru.
In the Śivasūtra.
In the pure sky, which is the constant flow of direct perception and whose inherent nature is ever-active;
Having plunged into the blissful one and bathed, he has completely washed away the impurities of the visible world.
Furthermore, in the *Svātmayogapradīpikā*, there is a verse (*vṛtta*):

I am that ocean of the nectar of infinite, true bliss and consciousness, from which the world of living beings subsists upon those drops of happiness brought by the wind of their own minds, produced by the collision of the multitude of waves known as the objects of the various sense organs.

Thus, having attained the state of non-duality, one realizes the true nature of the Great Guru of Supreme Knowledge— which has assumed the characteristic form of the water of the limbs of training, is free from the three sheaths, and is the very essence of supreme bliss.
In response to the inquiry "How so?", it is stated immediately thereafter: "The place of the water for washing the feet of knowledge. (76)
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Whatever may be uncovered in a person endowed with the five sense faculties.
His wisdom flows away, like water from the feet of a teacher. || 77 ||
In the Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad.

Therefore, I am eternally withdrawn from that [world]; I am its eternal awakening, its own inherent state of abiding; I am that which is peaceful, immovable, the mass of non-dual bliss and pure consciousness alone—that indeed is my supreme abode.

Thus ends the fourth section, titled "The Section on the Mobile Liṅga," within the *Liṅgasthalanirūpaṇa* of the *Kaivalyasāra*, which is a commentary on the *Ekottaraśatasthalashrutimālā* composed by the venerable Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of yogis of Śiva and wandering ascetic teacher.
The chapter is completed.
[The Fifth Chapter] | Salutations to the illustrious Śiva. Thus, the threefold nature of the *pādodaka-liṅga* and the *ekībhūta-liṅga*,
which constitutes the essential form of the accomplishment of refuge (*śaraṇa*) through right practice, has been explained according to its divisions.
In response to the inquiry "How so?", it is stated immediately thereafter that this is the locus for the accomplishment of action (kriyāniṣpattisthala).
