Then, such a Prāṇaliṅgin, through supreme bliss, having forgotten his own individual nature within the Liṅga of Grace resulting from spiritual transformation, takes refuge in the threefold Liṅgas of Perfection; and following the analogy of a devoted wife toward her husband, he restrains the enjoyment of all the senses and [abandons] the nature of Tamas.

Having set aside the threefoldness of the *ākāśaliṅga* and meditated upon it, standing at the place of instruction, one dispels the delusion of the body, the senses, and transmigratory existence; then, by perfecting one's conduct (*śīla*),
having become endowed with the threefoldness of the *prakāśaliṅga*, one effects the cessation of all karma and attains oneness with Śiva.
Having gone, he has attained the state of being a refuge. || 2 || [In the Kṣurikopaniṣad]
Just as at the time of extinction, a lamp, having burned out, goes to its dissolution.
In the same way, having burned away all karmas, the yogin shall go to Śiva. || 3 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Yogajagama:
The flower reveals the fruit; the fruit destroys the flower.
Action illuminates knowledge; knowledge destroys action.
Thus, having attained union with the limb of the refuge— the *liṅga* which has assumed the nature of the completion of the action—
it is characterized by being included within the state visible before the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
When the inquiry arises as to how it attains that nature of the completion of that state while having reached its differentiated form, [the following occurs] immediately thereafter.
This is called the locus for the perfection of contemplation, as stated in the Haṃsa Upaniṣad.

Therefore, when the mind has dissolved, when conceptualization and doubt have departed, and when merit and demerit are burnt away, the Vedic statement occurs: "Sadāśiva, whose nature is Śakti, being present everywhere, shines forth in peace. Furthermore, in the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad:
The mind is superior to the senses; the intellect (sattva) is higher than the mind.
The Self is greater than the sentient being, and the Unmanifest is greater than the Great One. || 7 ||
But beyond the unmanifest is the pervasive Puruṣa, who is indeed the subtle mark (liṅga).
Knowing which, a living being is liberated and attains immortality. || 8 ||
Again, in that very same place:
For the objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the objects.
The intellect (buddhi) is superior to the mind (manas), and the Great Self (mahān ātmā) is superior to the intellect. || 9 ||
Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest; beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa.
There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal.
It has been stated exactly thus in the Kirana Agama.
For those practitioners free from fatigue, it is accomplished after a long time.
For the stabilization of an entity is held to be the completion of that entity. || 11 ||
In the Śaivaratnākara.
When the state has been accomplished through the sequence of practice, one becomes a restrainer of mental fluctuations.
The supreme state of Śiva shines forth for the devotee whose mind has been stilled.
Thus, when the state [of reality] has been accomplished,

immediately after the destruction of the threefold refuge, one abides by oneself within the knowledge of that refuge; having attained the nature of the perfection of that knowledge, the distinctions [between subject and object] have ceased.
In response to the inquiry "How so?", the subsequent stage is described as the "place of the perfection of knowledge. (13)
In the Cūlikopaniṣad.
For one who possesses the eye of knowledge, all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects are clearly perceived.
The twice-born, being completely purified, behold him as one alone.
Furthermore, in the Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad:
Though cows possess many colors, their milk is of a single color.
Knowledge appears like milk to the possessor of the mark, just as it does to cows.
It has been stated exactly thus in the Yogasaṃgraha.
The perfection of knowledge is achieved through qualities such as selflessness and the like.
Certainty regarding that which touches the Supreme Self cannot arise from anything other than right knowledge. || 16 ||
In the *Tattvasāra*:
It is neither red nor yellow, neither white nor black.
It is completely free from all qualities, transcending multiplicity, and higher than the highest.
Thus, having attained the nature of the *piṇḍa* within the *piṇḍa* of the refuge—the unified sign characterized by the threefold signs of perfection—the question arises:
"How does that *piṇḍa* attain its partless nature? In response to this inquiry, the subsequent stage is called the "Space of the *Piṇḍa*" (*piṇḍākāśasthala*). || 18 ||
In the Aitareya Upaniṣad.

"O Prācīnayogin, worship Brahman, whose body is space, whose self is truth, who delights in the vital breaths, whose mind is bliss, who is perfected in peace, and who is immortal. Thus it has been said in the Śivarahasya as well.
Within the body is the supreme space, Śiva, who is higher than the highest.
Through the purification of all states of being, one should meditate; that is called the space of the body (piṇḍākāśa). || 20 ||
Furthermore, in the Sūktāvalī, the meter is [as follows]: vṛttam ||
To the one whose internal obstructions are dismantled by the thirty-six [principles] and who is endowed with the seven coverings, beginning with the skin;
Salutation for the sake of auspiciousness to the body that is the abode of Śiva, which exists as the liṅga whose essence is sound (nāda). || 21 ||

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to how the *liṅga*— which has attained a state of being a partless mass (*piṇḍa-niravayavatva*)— is of the nature of the space within the *bindu* situated in the center of the *piṇḍa* of the *śarīra*, the subsequent stage called the "Station of the Bindu-Space" (*bindvākāśasthala*) is described. || 22 ||
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
"He who lies within this space of the heart—he is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all. Furthermore, in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad:
This very one is the space within the heart; in it is this person consisting of mind, immortal, and golden.
24 || It has been stated likewise in the Kiraṇāgama:
Śiva is the pervasive cause of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Sadāśiva.
Śiva, whose form is the bindu, is to be meditated upon; he is called the Bindvākāśa (the Space of the Bindu). || 25 ||
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
Situated in the center of the bindu, it is subtle, hollow, and of the nature of light.
He, the self of all beings, beheld him who illuminates the path of peace.

Thus, having attained non-difference from that partless essential nature— the stainless *liṅga* called the *bindu*, which serves as the substratum for the consciousness that is the refuge and the objective of knowledge, wherein the distinction between knower and known has been discarded— [one attains liberation].
In response to the inquiry "How so?", it is stated immediately thereafter: "The great space-locus. (27)
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.
That is full, this is full; from the full, the great fullness arises.
Taking the fullness from the full, only fullness remains.
"Oṃ Khaṃ, Brahman is Khaṃ, the ancient. Thus it has been stated in the Vāsiṣṭha as well.
The entire sky is made by space; in space, space dissolves.
The void is enjoyed in the void; the eternal void [is enjoyed] in the void. || 29 ||
In that very same [text].
Because that which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts cannot be directly perceived.
By virtue of its being like the great space, everything is seen as it truly is.

Thus, regarding the inquiry as to how the threefold nature of the space-linga— which has become a single unified linga— attains its own luminosity within all the activities of the body despite having attained differentiation, [the following is stated] immediately thereafter.
This is called the section on the illumination of action in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.

"One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those who are performers of ritual action, learned in the Vedas, established in Brahman, offering oblations themselves to the Single Seer (Ekārṣi) with faith, and by whom that head-vow has been performed according to the rules. Thus it is likewise stated in the Śivarahasya.
With a state of supreme excellence and with minds that are serene and stainless.
And that cessation which is impelled is manifested as an action. || 33 ||
Furthermore, in the Rudrayāmala:
And for one who perceives the entire range of the visible world as nothing but Śiva, [there is no distinction].
The entire collection of ritual actions as well as the whole of the nature of consciousness would belong to that very [Self] alone. || 34 ||

Thus, in the process of action, having himself attained the very nature of action, the Liṅga— which is of the nature of light— having himself become the essential nature of being within the mental state of the seeker, attains luminosity; and when there arises the inquiry as to how this occurs, the subsequent stage is called the "Stage of the Illumination of Being" (bhāvaprakāśasthalam).
In the Haṃsa Upaniṣad: || 35 ||
That by which an entity is manifested and wherein an entity is dissolved—[that is Brahman].
Having realized "I am that Brahman," the self-controlled one becomes happy.
It has been stated in the same way in the Vijñānabhairava:
Then, by the illumination of the state of Śiva, the darkness of duality was destroyed.
Furthermore, that very same pure one manifests as Śiva alone. || 37 ||
Furthermore, in the Rudrayāmala:
Then, in the unstruck sound within the void, the mind becomes perfectly established simultaneously.
Devoted to the emptiness of beginning and end, the nature of Śiva shines forth.
And also in one's own realization.
If this is so, then the supreme reality, which is the inner self, has been revealed.
He attains his own supreme state, which is directly manifested. || 39 ||

Thus, when the sign (liṅga) has fallen away from being manifested by objective existence (bhāva), and having been cultivated through the state of the refuge (śaraṇa) as that which arises from existence,

immediately after the destruction of the triad (tripuṭī), one becomes great gnosis (mahājñāna) spontaneously; then, in response to the inquiry "how does one attain self-luminosity within oneself while free from duality?", [the following occurs] immediately thereafter:
It is called the locus of the illumination of knowledge; thus it is stated in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
This duality is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is non-dual.
If the imagined were negated by anyone, then conceptual construction would cease.
When the bond is known through instruction and other means, duality no longer exists. || 41 ||
Likewise, it has been stated in the Sūtasamhitā:
The Śruti, which speaks the truth, declares that duality consists of māyā.
And she declared the non-dual reality, which transcends all means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
When the knowledge of Brahman has arisen, which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the universe.
Everything shines as consisting of consciousness; nothing other than that is ever seen.
Even in one's own self-awareness.
The yogi should not think of anything at all; he should be intent on equanimity.
The reality does not manifest by itself merely through the absence of thought.

Thus ends the fifth section, titled "The Section on the Grace-Linga" (*prasādaliṅgasthala*), within the *Kaivalyasāra*— known as the *Commentary on the Garland of Scriptural Aphorisms on the One Hundred and One Sections* (*ekottaraśatasthalaśrutimālāvivaraṇa*)— composed by the illustrious Toṇṭadārya, the supreme king of Śiva-yogins and wandering ascetic teacher (*parivrājakācārya*). This concludes the exposition on the Section of the Linga (*liṅgasthalanirūpaṇa*) in the *Paramavīraśaivādvaitabodhinī*.
The chapter is concluded.
[The Sixth Chapter] | Homage to the illustrious Śiva. Thus, the *prakāśaliṅga*, having attained the state of being the grasper of transformation (*pariṇāma-grāhakatva*) within unity,
and that [unity] also, having attained the state of being the grasper of transformation within that *liṅga*—

In response to the inquiry as to how one who has attained a state where distinctions have vanished—by abandoning differentiated existence and undergoing transformation into supreme bliss—proceeds, it is stated immediately thereafter that he "occupies the stage of the accepted [state of] grace. (1)

Then, Śaraṇa, whose transformation into the *prasāda-liṅga* has thus occurred, being intent on attaining unity with the Great Liṅga (*mahāliṅga*) through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with the substratum, and being recognized as established in the threefold nature of the pervasive Liṅga (*vyāpaka-liṅga*),
[realizes that] in such a state of unity, there is indeed the perfection of all conduct.

Because it is the cause, having understood one's own true nature through the threefold signs of the presiding locus (*adhiṣṭhāna-liṅga*), and by means of the bestowed state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) in both sharing a single vessel and eating together, one becomes partless by abiding in the threefold signs that have transcended [duality]; thus it is established that permanence itself is the nature of Paraśiva. || 2 ||
In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

When for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? Then by what and whom should he smell? Then by what and whom should he cause to hear? Then by what and whom should he touch? Then by what and whom should he taste? Furthermore:
In the Vṛddhajābāla Upaniṣad.
The three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, are the remnants of the Blessed One's meal. Furthermore, in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad:

The great state called "dwelling in the cave" (guhācara) is present here; in this, all this is deposited—both that which is breath and that which is the twinkling of an eye. Furthermore, in the Talavakāra Upaniṣad:
"That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here.

That which one does not see with the eye, but by which the eyes see—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here. That which one does not hear with the ear, but by which this [ear]..."

"Know that very Brahman which you have heard; it is not this which they worship here. That by which one breathes through the vital breath (prāṇa), that by which the vital breath itself is made to breathe—that alone know thou to be Brahman; it is not this which they worship here. (6) Likewise it has been said in the *Śivayogadīpikā* [in an Āryā verse]:
Having taken up external objects through the pathways of the senses, the mind [is absorbed] in the ego-sense.
And she [the intellect] presents it to the Buddha (the pure consciousness); thereafter, the Person, the witness of the Buddha, experiences it.
Furthermore, in the Śivasūtra:
The offering of one's own self is the offering of all conceptual constructions into the abode of Śiva.
The bliss of the consciousness of Śiva consists of satisfaction, contraction, dissolution, and expansion. || 8 ||
In the *Liṅgasāra*:
I shall describe this threefold birth, consisting of its persistence, origination, and destruction.
The state of being offered after being intended, along with the three types of offering, is supreme.
It always has mental and physical afflictions as its great branches, and is perpetually invested with the threefold marks.
Childhood, youth, and old age—these three states are always offered to the Liṅga; they are always offered to the Liṅga. || 10 ||
Astonishment, the generation [of offspring], and sleep—all this is offered into the Liṅga.
The black, the white, and the yellow [forms] were themselves offered into the liṅga.
From birth until death, in all circumstances, amidst both pleasure and pain.
I am the renunciation of all prosperity, and all wealth has been offered to me.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Smṛti]:
The lord of yogis sees nothing else; he knows nothing else whatsoever.
When Śiva, who consists of the bliss of consciousness, is directly perceived, one hears nothing else.
In that very same place.
Neither desired nor abandoned, that which is to be known is attained by its very nature.
Objects of enjoyment are to be enjoyed just as rivers are by the ocean. || 14 ||

Thus, having embraced the bliss born from the serenity of supreme bliss—the mark of satisfaction in oneness—how is it that duality exists as one's own very form? In response to this inquiry, the subsequent section, "The Place of the Remnant of Food," is stated. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).
This, indeed, O Gārgī, is that imperishable which the Brāhmaṇas declare as neither coarse nor fine, neither short nor long; and then follows the instruction: "not this, not this."
It has been stated exactly so in the Vātula.
"Not this, not this"—that which remains as the supreme state after such negation.
Since it is impossible to deny [that], one should be happy, thinking "I am that. || 17 ||
In the *Candrāvalokana*.
For that whose sole essential nature is consciousness, there could never be any object of knowledge or the like.
Whatever exists, all that is considered to be composed of knowledge through its radiance.
Furthermore, in the Sūtasamhitā, there is a verse:
One should perceive Śiva through the instruction of the Guru, and one should also perceive Śiva through that very perception.
And having abandoned even the act of observation, only that which is one's own true nature—(that which remains as one's own consciousness)—remains as one's own consciousness alone. || 19 ||

Thus, when the Linga established in its own essential nature attains non-existence for both the moving and the unmoving within unity, the state where there is no longer existence of the moving and the unmoving is described immediately thereafter as the "state of the non-existence of the moving and the unmoving. (20)
In the Cūlikopaniṣad.
In whom all this—Brahman, both the stationary and the moving—is woven.
In that very [state] it goes to dissolution, just as bubbles [dissolve] in the ocean. || 21 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Vāsiṣṭha:
It is neither unity nor multiplicity; it is neither greatness nor minuteness.
Wherein the state of being felt—which is self-cognizable—is absent in both the moving and the unmoving.
In that very same [text].
Whatever exists in the world consisting of speech, whether the world be stationary or moving;
The entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, nothing exists apart from me.
Furthermore, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
Among worms, insects, and moths, as well as among stationary and moving beings;
There is no entity whatsoever that is ever established as a reality.

Thus, having established the threefold nature of the pervasive *liṅga* as the unified *liṅga*— which is the limb of all for oneness— and having shown that it has attained the state of being the locus and support for all the instruments and substances known as the various conducts (*sarvācāra*) while remaining merged within the vessel (*bhāṇḍa*), the "Stage of the Vessel" (*bhāṇḍasthala*) is described immediately thereafter to address the inquiry as to how its differentiation occurs. 25.
In the Kaivalya Upaniṣad.
Everything has arisen in me alone; everything is established in me.
Everything dissolves into me; therefore, I am that non-dual Brahman. || 26 ||
Furthermore, in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad:

"Or, that from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at their passing—that you should seek to understand; that is Brahman. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) Furthermore, in the Praśna Upaniṣad:
Consciousness is the Self; with all the gods, the vital breaths, and the elements, they are established therein.
O gentle one, he who knows that imperishable is omniscient and dwells within everything. 28.
It has been stated likewise in the Vātula:
In the midst of all renunciation, there is no knowledge that reveals the self.
Whatever vessel may be empty, he presides over it in each respective place. || 29 ||
In the *Stotrārṇava*, the meter is *vṛtta*.
My own body blossoms as the nature of existence, and all worlds attain the state of being my limbs.
All this, being permeated by duality, proceeds toward a state that does not even approach the domain of mindfulness and is unworthy of cultivation. 30.
Thus, having pervaded all causes—that is, all means of practice—the nature of the vessel is attained as the manifested sign (*liṅga*).

When the inquiry arises as to how that unity itself attains the state of being the vessel while its differentiation is attained, the "Stage of the Vessel" (*bhājanasthala*) is described immediately thereafter. || 31 ||
In the Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad.
With a golden vessel, he offered a gift to the person of truth.
O Nourisher, reveal that reality for the sake of seeing the true Dharma.
It has been stated likewise in the Vāsiṣṭha.
That which is indivisible and complete, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.
That by which it is made known is a corresponding cognition whose locus is non-different from itself. (33)
Furthermore, in the Śivadharmottara:
That which has been washed by the waters of knowledge and wiped clean by the bliss of one's own self.
That vessel is proclaimed to be the most excellent among all vessels. || 34 ||

Thus, when the Liṅga and the body have become non-distinct through their state of *sāmarasya* (perfect union), and the Liṅga has attained the quality of being an ointment (*lepatva*) over all the limbs of the body,

the subsequent stage— wherein the question arises as to how the distinction [between them] has been eliminated— is called "Anointing the Limbs" (*Aṅgalepanasthala*). This is stated in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.
In whom all this moves and vibrates, in whom all the gods have taken their seat. Furthermore, in the Dhyānabindu Upaniṣad:
Just as fragrance exists within a flower, and ghee exists within milk;
Just as oil exists within sesame seeds, and gold even within stone.
In this way, all beings are [bound] within the Self, like a gem on a thread.
Steady in intellect and undeluded, he is established in Brahman within Brahman.
Just as oil exists in sesame seeds and fragrance in a flower, so does it reside within its substratum.
Within the body of a person, however, he resides both externally and internally. || 39 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Vātula.
One's own supreme light, the manifest liṅga, exists both externally and internally.
Like oil appearing within sesame seeds, or like fire in the forest.
It resides within the self like clarified butter in milk, or like water in a stream.

Thus, having understood both "this" and "I" within the oneness of the threefold sign of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhānaliṅga*) as a single unified sign, when the inquiry arises as to how one who has attained duality [acts], the subsequent stage is called "the place of knowing oneself and others. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21)
Just as one embraced by a beloved woman knows nothing without nor within, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman), knows nothing without nor within; such is he.
Then, having attained desire, the form that desires the Self is desireless and beyond sorrow. Furthermore, in the Jābāla Upaniṣad:
He by whom it is not thought has understood it; he who thinks he knows it does not know it.
It is unknown to those who know it; it is known to those who do not know it. 43.
In the Sarvajñānottara.
The self is not other than itself, nor does anything other than itself exist.
Thus, even when that which is to be maintained has dissolved, for him there is indeed nothing to be known.
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
That is omniscience, that is auspiciousness, that is the state consisting of the supreme self.
That is truth and that is contentment wherein there is no looking toward oneself or others. 45.

In this way, when there arises the inquiry as to how one who has attained the realization of the oneness of the *liṅga*—characterized by the knowledge of both "this" and "I," and devoid of both [subject and object], yet still possesses a sense of difference—can be free from that duality, it is immediately stated:
"The state where existence and non-existence have perished. (Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad).
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one who is bound nor one who practices for liberation.
Neither one who desires liberation nor one who is liberated—this is the ultimate reality.
In the Yogaja-tantra:
It transcends the duality of existence and non-existence, and goes beyond both dreaming and waking.
Those who know reality recognize that reality as being free from both death and life.
Furthermore, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Rāmāyaṇa]:
When the sense of "I" does not exist, then indeed there is no egolessness.
That which is neither "I" nor "mine" is the destroyer of the notions of existence and non-existence.
In that very same [text].
Wherein there is neither the state of "you" nor "I," and no sense of otherness whatsoever.
Nowhere is there any conception of difference, nor any coloring by existence or non-existence.
Thus, having embraced the root-knowledge of oneness—which is the sign devoid of both existence and non-existence—that very knowledge itself becomes [the practitioner];

having remained in its own essential nature as that knowledge, how does it attain emptiness when distinctions have vanished? In response to this inquiry, the "Stage of Knowledge-Emptiness" (jñānaśūnyasthala) is described immediately thereafter.
In the Tejobindu Upaniṣad: || 51 ||
It is non-empty, yet its nature is emptiness; it abides in the heart, transcending emptiness.
It has not been meditated upon, nor has it been intensely contemplated; it is indeed that which is both the object of meditation and the non-object of meditation.
And every state that exists is empty—neither supreme, nor both supreme and non-supreme.
It is inconceivable and unawakened; it is neither real, nor do they know it as such. || 53 ||
It has been stated likewise in the Yogajagama:
Endowed with the conduct of knowledge, they have shaken off all impurities through knowledge.
The wise, through their state of being Śiva, partake in the unity of consciousness and the void.
Furthermore, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
Just as someone with a torch in hand might discard it after seeing an object, so too [should one abandon conceptualization].
Having illuminated the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should subsequently relinquish that knowledge itself.
In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā].
Where is there knowledge, and where is there action, for the Self which is changeless?
Since there are no external objects that can be perceived, this world is empty.
In the Kāmikāgama.
Just as clarified butter poured into clarified butter, or milk into milk;
Even if such isolation were attained, it would not be anything at all.
One perceives emptiness, again emptiness, and once more emptiness—the triple emptiness—in an instant.
Then there arises a state of equanimity that is entirely empty and free from appearances. || 58 ||
The one hundred and one sacred sites composed by Śrī Toṇṭadārya.
By reciting the *Kaivalyasāra*, one becomes a possessor of liberation immediately. || 59 ||
